stages.title: Beginner: from first note to first songs

units.title: Sound and pitch
units.summary: What a musical note is, why some notes sound high and others low, and what a fret does to a string.
units.whyItMatters: Knowing why a string sounds the way it does makes every later idea, from tuning to chords, make sense.

lessons.title: A sound is a vibration
lessons.teaches: Every sound is something vibrating, and a guitar note is a vibrating string made loud by the guitar.
facts: Sound is a vibration that travels through the air to your ear.
A plucked guitar string swings back and forth many times every second.
An acoustic guitar's hollow body makes the string's vibration loud enough to hear; an electric guitar uses a pickup and an amplifier instead.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Pluck open string 6 (the thickest string, low E) and watch it blur, then touch it lightly to stop it. Figure: fretboard with string 6 highlighted, plus audio of the open low E.

exercises.idea: A guitar string has to vibrate to make a sound (true).
What makes an acoustic guitar loud enough to hear: its hollow body, its tuning pegs, or its frets? (its body)
Pluck open string 6 and let it ring (E2); without a microphone, tap open string 6 on the neck picture.

lessons.title: Pitch: high and low
lessons.teaches: Pitch is how high or low a note sounds, and a faster vibration sounds higher.
facts: Pitch is how high or low a sound is.
A faster vibration sounds higher; a slower vibration sounds lower.
Vibration speed is measured in hertz (Hz): vibrations per second.
The open low E string vibrates about 82 times per second (82.4 Hz).
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play open string 6, then open string 1: both are called E, but string 1 sounds much higher. Figure: fretboard with strings 6 and 1 marked, audio of each.

exercises.idea: Two notes are played one after the other; was the second higher or lower?
Which vibrates faster: open string 6 or open string 1? (string 1)
A note that vibrates 220 times per second sounds lower than one that vibrates 110 times per second (false).

lessons.title: Loud is not high
lessons.teaches: Volume (how loud) and pitch (how high) are separate: plucking harder makes a note louder, not higher.
facts: Volume is how loud a sound is; it depends on how widely the string swings, not how fast.
Plucking harder makes a note louder, but it stays the same note.
Changes of volume in music are called dynamics.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Pluck open string 5 (A) very softly, then firmly: the same note at two volumes. Figure: audio of a soft and a loud A2, with a picture of a narrow and a wide string swing.

exercises.idea: The same string is played twice; did the pitch change or only the volume?
Plucking a string harder changes which note it plays (false).
Match each word to its meaning: pitch / how high or low; volume / how loud or soft; dynamics / changes of volume in music.

lessons.title: Frets make the string shorter
lessons.teaches: Pressing a string behind a fret shortens the part that vibrates, so the note sounds higher.
facts: A fret is a metal strip across the neck; pressing just behind it lets the string vibrate only from that fret to the bridge.
A shorter vibrating string vibrates faster and sounds higher.
Fret numbers count from the nut, the slotted strip where the strings leave the headstock (the end with the tuning pegs): fret 1 is the one closest to it.
Each fret toward the body raises the note by the same small step, called a half step.
lessons.onTheGuitar: On string 1, play open, then frets 1, 2 and 3: each note is a little higher. Figure: fretboard of string 1, frets 0 to 5, with the vibrating length shaded for each fret.

exercises.idea: Tap fret 3 on string 1.
Put these string 1 positions in order from lowest to highest pitch: fret 5, open, fret 3, fret 1.
Fret 1 is the fret nearest the body of the guitar (false).
Play string 1 at fret 3 (G4).
Play your first tune, "Hot Cross Buns" (traditional), on string 1 only: frets 4 2 0, 4 2 0, 0 0 0 0 2 2 2 2, 4 2 0. Higher frets give the higher notes.

lessons.title: The octave: the same note, higher
lessons.teaches: Two notes an octave apart sound like the same note at two heights, because one vibrates exactly twice as fast as the other.
facts: Two notes an octave apart share the same letter name.
The higher note of an octave vibrates exactly twice as fast as the lower note.
On any string, fret 12 sounds one octave above the open string.
Fret 12 sits halfway between the nut and the bridge.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play open string 6 (E2), then string 6 at fret 12 (E3), marked by the double dot on the neck. Figure: fretboard with string 6 frets 0 and 12 marked, audio of both.

exercises.idea: Two notes are played; are they an octave apart or not?
Tap the note one octave above open string 5 (string 5, fret 12).
An A vibrates 110 times per second. How fast does the A one octave higher vibrate? (220 times per second)
A note an octave higher has a different letter name (false).

lessons.title: Tone colour
lessons.teaches: Timbre (tone colour) is the character of a sound, which changes with the instrument and with where you pluck the string.
facts: Timbre, or tone colour, is what lets you tell a guitar from a piano playing the same note.
A plucked string vibrates in several ways at once, and the mix of those vibrations gives each instrument its own colour.
Plucking near the bridge gives a brighter, thinner tone; plucking over the end of the neck gives a warmer, rounder tone.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play string 3 at fret 2 (A3) plucked near the bridge, then plucked over the end of the neck. Figure: guitar body with the two picking zones marked; audio of both tones.

exercises.idea: The same note is plucked in two places; which one was plucked near the bridge (the brighter one)?
Changing where you pluck changes the name of the note (false).
Match: pitch / high or low; volume / loud or soft; timbre / tone colour.

units.checkpoint: Pitch versus volume versus tone colour; faster vibration means higher pitch; frets raise the pitch toward the body; the octave (same letter, twice the vibration speed, fret 12); hearing which of two notes is higher.

units.title: The six strings
units.summary: Number, name and tune the six open strings, and learn what "high", "low" and "up the neck" mean.
units.whyItMatters: Every chord chart, tab and lesson tells you where to play by string name or number.

lessons.title: String numbers
lessons.teaches: The strings are numbered 1 to 6, from the thinnest (highest) to the thickest (lowest).
facts: String 1 is the thinnest string; string 6 is the thickest.
String 1 sounds the highest and string 6 sounds the lowest.
When you hold the guitar to play, string 6 is the one nearest your face.
In tab and in this app's fretboard pictures, string 1 is drawn at the top.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard drawn the standard way (string 1 on top) with numbers 1 to 6 labelled, next to a picture of the neck as the player sees it looking down (string 6 nearest the eyes).

exercises.idea: Tap open string 4.
Which string is the thickest: string 1 or string 6? (6)
String 1 is the lowest-sounding string (false).

lessons.title: E A D G B E
lessons.teaches: In standard tuning the open strings, from string 6 to string 1, are E A D G B E.
facts: In standard tuning the open strings, from string 6 to string 1, are E A D G B E.
Strings 6 and 1 are both E, two octaves apart.
A memory sentence for the open strings from string 6 up: Every Apple Does Grow Big Eventually.
The set of notes the open strings are tuned to is called a tuning; E A D G B E is standard tuning, the one most songs and lessons use.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard with each open string labelled with its name and number; audio plays the open strings from 6 to 1.

exercises.idea: Put the open strings in order from string 6 to string 1.
Which note is open string 3? (G)
Complete the tuning from string 6: E A _ G _ E (D, B).
Play the open string named D (string 4, D3).

lessons.title: Using a tuner
lessons.teaches: A tuner names the nearest note and shows whether the string is too low (flat) or too high (sharp); tighten to raise, loosen to lower.
facts: In tuning, flat means slightly too low and sharp means slightly too high.
Tightening a string raises its pitch; loosening it lowers its pitch.
Standard tuning sounds E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4; the number after the letter tells which octave the note is in.
Octave numbers go up by one at each C: the note just above B3 is C4.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: a tuner face reading "A" with the needle left of centre (flat) over string 5; audio reference tones for each open string.

exercises.idea: Your tuner says D and the needle is left of centre (flat). Tighten or loosen the string? (tighten)
Loosening a string raises its pitch (false).
Match each string to its sounding pitch: 6 / E2, 5 / A2, 4 / D3, 3 / G3, 2 / B3, 1 / E4.
Tune and play open string 5 (A2).

lessons.title: The fifth-fret rule
lessons.teaches: Fret 5 of each string matches the next thinner open string, except on string 3, where fret 4 does.
facts: String 6 at fret 5 is A, the same note as open string 5.
Fret 5 matches the next thinner open string on strings 6, 5, 4 and 2.
On string 3 (G), fret 4 is B, the same note as open string 2.
Two notes at exactly the same pitch are in unison; slightly out of tune, they make a wobbling sound called beating.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard with fret 5 on strings 6, 5, 4 and 2 and fret 4 on string 3 joined by arrows to the next open string; audio of each pair played together.

exercises.idea: Tap the fret on string 4 that matches open string 3 (fret 5).
Which fret on string 3 matches open string 2? (fret 4)
Two strings are played together; are they in tune (steady) or out of tune (wobbling)?
Play string 6 at fret 5; it should match open string 5 (A2).

lessons.title: High, low and up the neck
lessons.teaches: On the guitar, "high" and "up" mean higher in pitch, so "up the neck" means toward the body.
facts: "Higher" on the guitar means higher in pitch, not higher in space.
Moving up the neck means moving toward the body, to higher-pitched frets.
The "low E" string is string 6 and the "high E" string is string 1.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: neck with an arrow labelled "up the neck" pointing from the nut toward the body, and strings 6 (low E) and 1 (high E) labelled.

exercises.idea: Moving up the neck means moving toward the headstock (false).
Your teacher says "play the same note higher up the neck". Which way does your hand move? (toward the body)
A dot is shown on open string 1; name the note (E, the high E string).

units.checkpoint: String numbers 1 to 6; the open-string names E A D G B E from string 6 to 1 and what standard tuning is; flat and sharp on a tuner, tighten to raise; the fifth-fret rule with fret 4 on string 3; up the neck means toward the body.

units.title: The musical alphabet
units.summary: The seven letter names, half and whole steps, sharps, flats and the twelve notes.
units.whyItMatters: With twelve note names you can find, name and talk about every note on the guitar.

lessons.title: Seven letters, round and round
lessons.teaches: Notes are named with the letters A to G, and after G the letters start again at A, an octave higher.
facts: The musical alphabet has seven letters: A B C D E F G.
After G comes A again, one octave higher than the first A.
A note named with just a letter, with no sharp or flat, is called a natural note.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 5 from open to fret 12 with the natural notes A B C D E F G A marked at frets 0, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12; a keyboard with the white keys lettered.

exercises.idea: Complete: C D _ F _ A _ (E, G, B).
Which letter comes after G? (A)
Arrange these so they rise from C: F, D, G, E (D E F G).

lessons.title: Half steps and whole steps
lessons.teaches: A half step is the distance of one fret, and a whole step is two frets.
facts: A half step (also called a semitone) is the distance of one fret.
A whole step (also called a tone) is two half steps: two frets.
On a piano a half step is from one key to the very next key, black or white.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 1, frets 0 to 4, with a half-step arrow from fret 0 to 1 and a whole-step arrow from fret 1 to 3; a keyboard showing the same steps.

exercises.idea: From fret 3 to fret 5 on one string is a half step or a whole step? (whole step)
Tap the note a whole step above string 6 fret 3 on the same string (fret 5).
A whole step is two frets (true).
Two notes are played one after the other: a half step or a whole step apart?

lessons.title: The two natural half steps
lessons.teaches: Most neighbouring letters are a whole step apart, but E-F and B-C are only a half step apart.
facts: E to F is a half step: there is no note between them.
B to C is a half step: there is no note between them.
The other neighbouring natural notes (C-D, D-E, F-G, G-A, A-B) are a whole step apart.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 6 from open to fret 12 with the natural notes E (0), F (1), G (3), A (5), B (7), C (8), D (10), E (12); the E-F and B-C pairs sit on neighbouring frets. A keyboard shows no black key between E-F and B-C.

exercises.idea: On string 6, tap F (fret 1).
Which pair is only a half step apart: B-C, C-D or A-B? (B-C)
There is a note between E and F (false).
On string 5, tap C (fret 3).
Two pairs of notes are played, E-F and F-G: which pair was the half step?

lessons.title: Sharps raise by a half step
lessons.teaches: A sharp (#) raises a note by one half step, one fret higher.
facts: A sharp (#) raises a note by a half step: one fret higher.
F# (F sharp) is one fret above F.
The note between two natural notes a whole step apart can be named as the sharp of the lower one: between F and G is F#.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 6 with F at fret 1, F# at fret 2, G at fret 3 and G# at fret 4.

exercises.idea: Tap G# on string 6 (fret 4).
Name the note at string 6, fret 2, using a sharp (F#).
C# is one fret above C or one fret below C? (above)

lessons.title: Flats lower by a half step
lessons.teaches: A flat (b) lowers a note by one half step, one fret lower.
facts: A flat (b) lowers a note by a half step: one fret lower.
Bb (B flat) is one fret below B.
Sharp and flat signs are both called accidentals.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 5 with Bb at fret 1 and B at fret 2; string 6 with Ab at fret 4 and A at fret 5.

exercises.idea: Tap Bb on string 5 (fret 1).
Name the note at string 6, fret 4, using a flat (Ab).
Eb is one fret below E (true).

lessons.title: One sound, two names
lessons.teaches: F# and Gb are the same pitch with two names; such notes are called enharmonic equivalents.
facts: Two names for the same pitch are called enharmonic equivalents, or enharmonics.
F# and Gb sound the same and are played at the same fret.
The five notes between the natural notes are C#/Db, D#/Eb, F#/Gb, G#/Ab and A#/Bb.
Which of the two names is correct depends on the key or chord; the rules come with scales.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 6 from open to fret 12 with all twelve notes; the in-between frets carry both names (F#/Gb at fret 2, G#/Ab at fret 4, A#/Bb at fret 6, C#/Db at fret 9, D#/Eb at fret 11).

exercises.idea: Pair each sharp with the flat that sounds the same: C#/Db, D#/Eb, F#/Gb, G#/Ab, A#/Bb.
Which note sounds the same as A#? (Bb)
Tap Db on string 5 (fret 4).

lessons.title: The twelve notes
lessons.teaches: There are twelve different notes in an octave, so twelve half steps (twelve frets) bring you back to the same letter.
facts: Most Western music uses twelve different notes in each octave; then the pattern repeats.
Twelve half steps make one octave, which is why fret 12 is the octave of the open string.
Playing all the notes in a row, one fret at a time, is called the chromatic scale.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 1 from open to fret 12, each fret lighting up as the audio plays the chromatic scale from E4 to E5.

exercises.idea: Arrange the notes of string 1 from open to fret 5: E, F, F#, G, G#, A.
Complete the chromatic scale: A A# B C _ D D# E F _ G G# A (C#, F#).
Play string 1 from open to fret 5, one fret at a time.
How many half steps make an octave? (12)

units.checkpoint: The seven letters in order and wrapping from G to A; half step = one fret, whole step = two frets; the natural half steps E-F and B-C; sharps raise and flats lower by a half step; the five enharmonic pairs; twelve notes in an octave; naming frets 0 to 5 on string 6.

units.title: Pulse and beat
units.summary: The steady beat, tempo, bars of 4/4, the first note values and rests, and down-up strumming.
units.whyItMatters: Playing in time is what makes a few simple chords sound like real music.

lessons.title: The beat
lessons.teaches: The beat (pulse) is the steady, evenly spaced count you tap your foot to.
facts: The beat, or pulse, is the steady count underneath music that you tap your foot to.
Beats are evenly spaced in time, like the tick of a clock.
A metronome is a device or app that clicks a steady beat.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Lay your fretting hand flat across all six strings around frets 1 to 3, without pressing, so they are muted (a light touch right over fret 5, 7 or 12 would ring a harmonic instead), and strum once on every click at 60 BPM. Figure: rhythm line of four evenly spaced beats; audio click.

exercises.idea: Tap along with a click at 70 BPM for eight beats.
Two click tracks: which one is steady?
Beats are evenly spaced in time (true).

lessons.title: Tempo and BPM
lessons.teaches: Tempo is the speed of the beat, measured in beats per minute (BPM).
facts: Tempo is the speed of the beat.
Tempo is measured in beats per minute (BPM): at 60 BPM there is one beat every second.
At 120 BPM the beats come twice as fast as at 60 BPM.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum the six muted strings (fretting hand resting flat around frets 1 to 3) on every click at 60, then 90, then 120 BPM; then pick open string 6 on every click. Figure: metronome with its BPM dial; audio at each tempo.

exercises.idea: At 60 BPM, how many beats happen each second? (1)
Two click tracks: which is faster?
Tap quarter notes with the click at 90 BPM.

lessons.title: Bars and counting to four
lessons.teaches: Beats are grouped into bars; in 4/4 time each bar has four beats and beat 1 is the strongest.
facts: Music groups beats into bars (also called measures), separated by bar lines.
In 4/4 time there are four beats in every bar, counted 1 2 3 4.
Beat 1 of a bar is called the downbeat and usually feels the strongest.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Pick open string 6 (low E) on beat 1 and strum the muted strings on beats 2, 3 and 4 while counting "1 2 3 4" aloud. Figure: rhythm line of two 4/4 bars with bar lines and beat numbers; audio click with beat 1 accented.

exercises.idea: Tap only beat 1 of each bar for four bars of 4/4 at 80 BPM.
How many beats are in a bar of 4/4? (4)
Clicks with an accent on beat 1: are the bars four beats or three beats long?

lessons.title: Quarter, half and whole notes
lessons.teaches: In 4/4 a quarter note lasts one beat, a half note two beats and a whole note four beats.
facts: In 4/4 time a quarter note lasts one beat.
A half note lasts as long as two quarter notes: two beats in 4/4.
A whole note lasts as long as four quarter notes: a whole bar of 4/4.
A quarter note has a filled-in head and a stem, a half note a hollow head and a stem, and a whole note a hollow head and no stem.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum open strings: four quarter notes, then two half notes (let them ring), then one whole note. Figure: rhythm line of three bars (quarters, halves, a whole note); audio.

exercises.idea: Tap one bar: half note, quarter note, quarter note.
How many beats does a half note last in 4/4? (2)
Match each note value to its length in 4/4: whole / 4 beats, half / 2 beats, quarter / 1 beat.

lessons.title: Eighth notes and the "&"
lessons.teaches: Two eighth notes fit in one beat, counted "1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &".
facts: Two eighth notes last as long as one quarter note.
Eighth notes are counted 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 &; each "&" falls exactly halfway between two beats.
A single eighth note has one flag; eighth notes in a group are joined by one beam.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum open strings 3, 2 and 1 down on every number and up on every "&" at 70 BPM. Figure: rhythm line of eight eighth notes with counts and down/up arrows under them; audio.

exercises.idea: Tap one bar of eighth notes at 70 BPM.
Count a bar of eighth notes: 1 & 2 _ 3 & _ & (&, 4).
How many eighth notes fill a bar of 4/4? (8)

lessons.title: Rests: counted silence
lessons.teaches: A rest is a silence of an exact length, and each note value has a matching rest.
facts: A rest is a silence that lasts an exact number of beats.
Each note value has a matching rest: whole, half, quarter and eighth rests.
A whole rest is a small block that hangs down from a line; a half rest is the same block sitting on top of a line.
A whole rest is also used for a whole bar of silence, however many beats the bar has.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum open strings 3, 2 and 1 on beats 1 and 3, and stop them with the side of your picking hand on beats 2 and 4. Figure: rhythm line of quarter, quarter rest, quarter, quarter rest, plus the four rest symbols; audio.

exercises.idea: Tap one bar: quarter, quarter rest, quarter, quarter.
Match each rest symbol to its name (whole, half, quarter, eighth).
How long does a quarter rest last in 4/4? (1 beat)

lessons.title: Down on the beat, up on the "&"
lessons.teaches: In eighth-note strumming the hand moves down on every beat and up on every "&", even when it skips the strings.
facts: In eighth-note strumming, downstrokes fall on the beats and upstrokes on the "&"s.
To leave out a strum, keep the hand moving and swing past the strings without touching them.
A hand that never stops moving down and up is what keeps strumming steady.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum open strings (or Em, 022000: strings 5 and 4 at fret 2, the rest open) with the pattern down (1), down-up (2 &), up (&), down-up (4 &), missing the strings on beat 3. Figure: rhythm line with the counts and down/up arrows, the silent beat 3 greyed out; audio.

exercises.idea: Tap the pattern on 1, 2, & of 2, & of 3, 4, & of 4.
Place the strums of the pattern "down, down-up, up, down-up" on the counts 1 2 & 3 & 4 &.
In eighth-note strumming, upstrokes fall on the numbers (false).

units.checkpoint: Beat versus tempo and BPM; bars, bar lines and the downbeat in 4/4; whole, half, quarter and eighth notes with their rests and their lengths in 4/4; counting 1 & 2 &; tapping a bar of quarters, eighths and rests at 70 to 90 BPM; downstrokes on the beat and upstrokes on the &.

units.title: Reading tab
units.summary: Read guitar tablature: strings, frets, chords, technique symbols and rhythm.
units.whyItMatters: Tab is the quickest way to read guitar music, and most guitar parts you find are written in it.

lessons.title: Six lines, six strings
lessons.teaches: Tab has six lines, one per string, with string 1 (high E) on top.
facts: Tab (tablature) shows guitar music on six lines, one for each string.
The top line of tab is string 1 (high E) and the bottom line is string 6 (low E).
Tab is often labelled e B G D A E from the top line down.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: six empty tab lines beside a fretboard diagram, each line joined to its string: top line string 1 (e), then string 2 (B), string 3 (G), string 4 (D), string 5 (A) and the bottom line string 6 (E).

exercises.idea: Which string is the bottom line of tab? (string 6, low E)
Match tab lines to strings: top / string 1, second / string 2, third / string 3, bottom / string 6.
The top line of tab is the thickest string (false).

lessons.title: Numbers are frets
lessons.teaches: A number on a tab line is the fret to press on that string, and 0 means play it open.
facts: A number on a tab line is the fret to press on that string.
A 0 means play the string open, with no fret pressed.
Tab is read from left to right, like text.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab snippet string 1 fret 0, string 1 fret 1, string 1 fret 3, string 2 fret 1; a fretboard lights each position as audio plays E4 F4 G4 C4.

exercises.idea: The tab shows a 3 on the second line from the top; tap that position (string 2, fret 3).
Play the four-note tab snippet.
What does a 0 on the bottom line mean? (play open string 6)

lessons.title: Numbers in a column
lessons.teaches: Numbers lined up in one column are played together, which is how tab writes a chord.
facts: Numbers stacked in one column are played at the same time.
Tab writes a chord as a column of numbers, one for each string that sounds.
In tab, an x on a line is a muted note: the string is touched to deaden it and struck for a percussive click.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab column reading 0 1 0 2 3 from the top line down with nothing on the bottom line, which is the open C chord, written x32010 (frets from string 6 to string 1, x for a string not played), next to its chord box; audio strum.

exercises.idea: Place your fingers for the tab column 0 1 0 2 3 (strings 1 to 5), string 6 not played.
Three numbers in one column are played one after another, or together? (together)
An x in tab means play that string open (false).

lessons.title: Slides, hammers and bends
lessons.teaches: Tab marks playing techniques with letters and symbols between or after the fret numbers.
facts: h means hammer-on: sound a higher note on the same string by bringing a finger down, without picking again.
p means pull-off: sound a lower note on the same string by pulling a finger off, without picking again.
/ means slide up and \ means slide down along the string.
b means bend: 7b9 means pick fret 7 and push the string sideways until it sounds like fret 9.
~ means vibrato: a quick, even wobble of the pitch.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab on string 3 showing 5h7, then 7p5, then 5/7, then 7b9 with a bend arrow; audio of each.

exercises.idea: Match each symbol to its technique: h / hammer-on, p / pull-off, / / slide up, b / bend, ~ / vibrato.
In 5h7, how many times do you pick the string? (once)
Play 5h7 on string 3, picking only once.

lessons.title: What tab does not tell you
lessons.teaches: Plain tab shows where to play but usually not how long each note lasts, so rhythm comes from stems under the tab, notation or listening.
facts: Plain tab shows the string and fret but usually not how long each note lasts.
Some tab adds stems and beams under the numbers to show rhythm with ordinary note values.
The spacing between numbers in plain tab is only a rough guide to timing.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the same four-note line on string 1 (0 1 3 1) twice: plain tab, then tab with rhythm stems (quarter, quarter, half, then a whole note in the next bar); audio of both.

exercises.idea: Hear a short line and pick the tab with the matching rhythm stems.
Plain tab always shows the exact rhythm (false).
Tap the rhythm shown under the tab: quarter, quarter, half.

lessons.title: Your first tab tune
lessons.teaches: A melody is a line of single notes, built from phrases, and tab lets you play one by reading string and fret for each note.
facts: A melody is a series of single notes heard as a tune.
A phrase is a musical sentence; many melodies are built from four-bar phrases.
One melody often moves between strings: the tab tells you which string each note is on.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab of the first four-bar phrase of Beethoven's "Ode to Joy" (public domain) in C on strings 1 and 2: bar 1 string 1 frets 0 0 1 3; bar 2 string 1 frets 3 1 0, string 2 fret 3; bar 3 string 2 frets 1 1 3, string 1 fret 0; bar 4 string 1 fret 0, string 2 frets 3 3. Audio at 70 BPM.

exercises.idea: Play the first phrase of "Ode to Joy" from the tab at 70 BPM.
Tap the highest note of the phrase (string 1, fret 3, G).
Put the four notes of bar 2 in order from the tab (string 1 fret 3, string 1 fret 1, string 1 fret 0, string 2 fret 3).

units.checkpoint: Tab lines are strings with string 1 on top; numbers are frets, 0 is open; a column is played together; x is a muted note; h, p, /, \, b and ~; plain tab usually leaves out rhythm; reading and playing a four-bar tab phrase.

units.title: Notes on the neck
units.summary: Name the notes on strings 6 and 5, use the dots and fret 12 as landmarks, and find octaves with shapes.
units.whyItMatters: Knowing where the notes are lets you find any chord, scale or riff instead of memorising positions blindly.

lessons.title: The natural notes on string 6
lessons.teaches: On string 6 the natural notes are E (open), F (1), G (3), A (5), B (7), C (8), D (10) and E (12).
facts: On string 6 the natural notes are E (open), F (1), G (3), A (5), B (7), C (8), D (10) and E (12).
String 1 has its notes at the same frets as string 6, because both are E strings.
Many movable chord shapes are named after their lowest note on string 6 or string 5.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard of string 6, frets 0 to 12, with the natural notes labelled and the rest left blank; audio as each is tapped.

exercises.idea: Tap A on string 6 (fret 5).
Name the note at string 6, fret 8 (C).
Type the fret number of G on string 6 (3).

lessons.title: The natural notes on string 5
lessons.teaches: On string 5 the natural notes are A (open), B (2), C (3), D (5), E (7), F (8), G (10) and A (12).
facts: On string 5 the natural notes are A (open), B (2), C (3), D (5), E (7), F (8), G (10) and A (12).
A note on string 5 is the same pitch as string 6 five frets higher.
Once you know a natural note, its sharp is one fret up and its flat one fret down.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard of strings 6 and 5, frets 0 to 12, string 5 naturals labelled; string 5 fret 3 (C) linked to string 6 fret 8 (C).

exercises.idea: Tap D on string 5 (fret 5).
Name string 5, fret 4 (C# or Db).
Play E on string 5 (fret 7, E3).

lessons.title: The neck repeats at fret 12
lessons.teaches: From fret 12 up, every string repeats its notes an octave higher, so fret 15 has the same name as fret 3.
facts: Every note at fret 12 or above has the same name as the note twelve frets lower, one octave higher.
The note at fret 15 has the same name as the note at fret 3.
Fret 12 of each string has the same name as the open string.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 6, frets 0 to 15, with frets 0 to 3 and 12 to 15 highlighted in matching colours (E F F# G and E F F# G).

exercises.idea: Name string 5, fret 15 (C).
Which fret on string 6 has the same note name as fret 17? (fret 5, A)
Tap a G on string 6 above fret 12 (fret 15).

lessons.title: The dots as landmarks
lessons.teaches: The dot markers at frets 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12 are landmarks you can name notes from.
facts: Most guitars have dot markers at frets 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12 (a double dot at 12), repeating at 15, 17, 19 and 21 on longer necks, with another double dot at 24 on 24-fret necks; some classical guitars have them only on the side of the neck.
On string 6 the dots fall on G (3), A (5), B (7) and C# (9).
On string 5 the dots fall on C (3), D (5), E (7) and F# (9).
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard frets 0 to 12 with the inlay dots drawn and the string 6 and string 5 notes at frets 3, 5, 7, 9 labelled.

exercises.idea: Name the note at string 6 on the 9th-fret dot (C#).
Tap the note on string 5 at the 7th-fret dot (E).
On string 5 the 5th-fret dot is D (true).

lessons.title: The same note in several places
lessons.teaches: The same pitch can be played in several places: on the next thinner string it is five frets lower, or four frets lower when crossing from string 3 to string 2.
facts: The same pitch can usually be played in more than one place on the neck.
String 6 at fret 5 and open string 5 are the same A (A2).
To play the same pitch on the next thinner string, go five frets lower; crossing from string 3 to string 2, go four frets lower.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard frets 0 to 12 with the three places D3 can be played: string 6 fret 10, string 5 fret 5 and open string 4.

exercises.idea: Tap every place the pitch D3 can be played between frets 0 and 12 (string 6 fret 10, string 5 fret 5, string 4 open).
String 3 fret 7 (D4) is the same pitch as which fret on string 2? (fret 3)
Play A2 in two different places (string 6 fret 5, open string 5).
Two positions are played one after the other: the same pitch, or an octave apart?

lessons.title: Octave shapes from strings 6 and 5
lessons.teaches: The octave above a note on string 6 or 5 is two strings thinner and two frets higher.
facts: From a note on string 6, the octave above is on string 4, two frets higher.
From a note on string 5, the octave above is on string 3, two frets higher.
Octave shapes let you name notes on strings 4 and 3 from the ones you know on strings 6 and 5.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard with string 6 fret 3 (G2) joined to string 4 fret 5 (G3), and string 5 fret 3 (C3) joined to string 3 fret 5 (C4); the string between is muted.

exercises.idea: Tap the octave above string 6, fret 5 (string 4, fret 7).
Name the note at string 4, fret 7 (A).
Play the C an octave above string 5 fret 3 (string 3 fret 5, C4).
Two notes are played: is the second an octave above the first?

lessons.title: Octave shapes across the B string
lessons.teaches: The octave above a note on string 4 or 3 is two strings thinner and three frets higher, because strings 3 and 2 are tuned closer together than the other pairs.
facts: From a note on string 4, the octave above is on string 2, three frets higher.
From a note on string 3, the octave above is on string 1, three frets higher.
The extra fret comes from the B string: strings 3 and 2 are four half steps apart, while every other neighbouring pair is five.
String 6 and string 1 at the same fret are two octaves apart.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard with string 4 fret 2 (E3) joined to string 2 fret 5 (E4), and string 3 fret 2 (A3) joined to string 1 fret 5 (A4).

exercises.idea: Tap the octave above string 3, fret 4 (string 1, fret 7).
Name the note at string 2, fret 5 (E).
From string 4 the octave shape is two frets up, the same as from string 6 (false).

units.checkpoint: Naming and finding the natural notes on strings 6 and 5 up to fret 12; the repeat at fret 12; dot landmarks; the same pitch five frets back on the next string (four across strings 3 and 2); octave shapes 6 to 4 and 5 to 3 (two frets up) and 4 to 2 and 3 to 1 (three frets up); naming sharps and flats from the naturals.

units.title: Your first scale
units.summary: What a scale is, and the A minor pentatonic scale in the shape guitarists use most.
units.whyItMatters: With one five-note shape you can already play melodies and solos that sound like real guitar music.

lessons.title: What a scale is
lessons.teaches: A scale is a set of notes in order of pitch, built from a home note called the tonic, after which it is named.
facts: A scale is a set of notes arranged in order of pitch.
The home note of a scale is its tonic, and the scale is named after it.
Different scales choose different notes, which gives each scale its own sound.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Audio: A minor pentatonic up and down from A2, then the same notes in a jumble that stops on D. Figure: fretboard of string 5 with the scale notes lit.

exercises.idea: Two short tunes use the same notes; which ending sounds finished (the one ending on the tonic)?
A scale is named after its tonic (true).
What is the home note of a scale called? (the tonic)

lessons.title: Five notes: A C D E G
lessons.teaches: The A minor pentatonic scale has five notes: A C D E G.
facts: The A minor pentatonic scale has five notes: A C D E G.
"Pentatonic" means five notes ("penta" is Greek for five).
The minor pentatonic is one of the most used scales in rock, blues and pop guitar.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 5 from open to fret 12 with A C D E G A at frets 0, 3, 5, 7, 10, 12; audio ascending.

exercises.idea: Complete A minor pentatonic: A _ D E _ (C, G).
On string 5, tap every note of A minor pentatonic from open to fret 12.
Which note is not in A minor pentatonic: C, D or F? (F)

lessons.title: The box at fret 5
lessons.teaches: The most used shape of A minor pentatonic covers frets 5 to 8 on all six strings.
facts: A minor pentatonic box 1 uses frets 5 and 8 on strings 6, 2 and 1, and frets 5 and 7 on strings 5, 4 and 3.
Many players call this shape box 1 (or position 1) of the minor pentatonic; its lowest note is the tonic.
A common fingering: first finger on fret 5, third finger on fret 7, fourth finger on fret 8.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard frets 4 to 9 with box 1 marked (6: 5, 8; 5: 5, 7; 4: 5, 7; 3: 5, 7; 2: 5, 8; 1: 5, 8) and finger numbers; tab of the box ascending; audio.

exercises.idea: Play the box from its lowest note to its highest, one note at a time.
Tap every note of the box.
Put the box notes in playing order from the lowest string up.

lessons.title: Where the roots are
lessons.teaches: Box 1 of A minor pentatonic contains three A notes, and phrases that end on one of them sound settled.
facts: In box 1 of A minor pentatonic the A notes are at string 6 fret 5, string 4 fret 7 and string 1 fret 5.
Guitarists often call the tonic notes inside a scale shape its roots.
Ending a phrase on the root makes it sound settled.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: box 1 with the three roots in the root colour (string 6 fret 5, string 4 fret 7, string 1 fret 5) and the other notes plain.

exercises.idea: Tap all three A notes in the box.
Two phrases from the box: which ends on the root?
Play a short phrase of your own from the box that ends on string 4, fret 7.

lessons.title: Move the box, change the key
lessons.teaches: Sliding the box along the neck keeps its shape and changes its tonic, and with it the key (which note is home): the tonic is the note under your first finger on string 6.
facts: Moving the whole box along the neck keeps the shape and changes the tonic.
The tonic is the string 6 note under the first finger: at fret 3 the box is G minor pentatonic, at fret 8 C minor pentatonic.
Each fret you move the box changes the tonic by a half step.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: box 1 drawn at fret 5 (A), fret 3 (G) and fret 8 (C), with the string 6 root labelled each time.

exercises.idea: Box 1 with the first finger at fret 7 on string 6 is which minor pentatonic? (B)
Tap the string 6 root for box 1 of D minor pentatonic (fret 10).
Box 1 starts at string 6, fret 12. Which minor pentatonic is it? (E)

lessons.title: Making music with five notes
lessons.teaches: Short repeated ideas, space between phrases and endings on the root turn a scale into music.
facts: Repeating a short idea and then changing its ending is the simplest way to make a melody sound intentional.
Leaving silence between phrases sounds musical; you do not have to play all the time.
In A minor, ending on A sounds the most at rest.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab of an original two-bar phrase written for this lesson in box 1, played twice: the first time ending on D (string 3 fret 7), the second ending on A (string 4 fret 7); audio over an A drone (a low A that keeps sounding).

exercises.idea: Play the phrase, then play it again changing only the last note to a root.
Which version of the phrase sounds finished?
A good solo uses every note of the box in every bar (false).

units.checkpoint: What a scale and its tonic are; the five notes of A minor pentatonic; the box-1 shape at fret 5 (frets 5 and 8 on strings 6, 2, 1; 5 and 7 on strings 5, 4, 3); its three roots; moving the box to other keys by the string-6 root; ending a phrase on the root.

units.title: Why a chord is major or minor
units.summary: What a chord is, how to read a chord box, and the one note that makes a chord major or minor.
units.whyItMatters: Once you see the third, every open chord you learn makes sense, and you can fix a wrong chord by ear.

lessons.title: What a chord is
lessons.teaches: A chord is several notes played together, named after its root, and guitarists write a chord shape as six fret numbers from string 6 to string 1.
facts: A chord is several different notes sounding together; most chords have at least three.
The note a chord is named after is its root.
Chord shapes are often written as six characters from string 6 to string 1: Em is 022000 (strings 5 and 4 at fret 2, the rest open).
In that spelling an x marks a string that is not played: open C is x32010.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum Em (022000): string 5 and string 4 at fret 2, all other strings open. Figure: the Em tab column (0 0 0 2 2 0 from the top line down) beside its six-character spelling 022000, read from string 6 to string 1; audio strum.

exercises.idea: Strum Em (022000).
In the spelling 022000, which string does the first character describe? (string 6, the thickest)
A chord is one note played loudly (false).
Did you hear one note or a chord?

lessons.title: Reading a chord box
lessons.teaches: A chord box is a picture of the neck that shows where each finger goes: strings run down, frets run across, and o and x mark open and unplayed strings.
facts: In a chord box the vertical lines are strings (string 6 on the left) and the horizontal lines are frets, with the nut at the top.
In a chord box a dot is a finger, o means play the string open and x means do not play it.
Numbers on or under the dots name the fingers: 1 index, 2 middle, 3 ring, 4 little finger.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord boxes of Em (022000: fingers 2 and 3 on strings 5 and 4 at fret 2) and C (x32010: x over string 6, finger 3 on string 5 fret 3, finger 2 on string 4 fret 2, finger 1 on string 2 fret 1), each beside the same shape on a fretboard; audio strum.

exercises.idea: Place Em from its chord box: string 5 fret 2 and string 4 fret 2, all other strings open.
In a chord box, which side is string 6? (the left)
An x above a string in a chord box means play it open (false).
Place C from its chord box (x32010), leaving string 6 unplayed.
In the C chord box (x32010), how many strings are played? (5)

lessons.title: Root, third and fifth
lessons.teaches: A triad is built from a root, the note a third above it and the note a fifth above it, found by counting letter names.
facts: A triad is a three-note chord made of a root, a third and a fifth.
Count letter names from the root, counting the root as 1: in C D E F G, E is the third and G is the fifth.
A C major chord is made of C, E and G.
Guitar chords often repeat triad notes on several strings: open C (x32010) plays C E G C E.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord box of C (x32010) with each dot labelled R, 3 or 5 (string 5 fret 3 = C, string 4 fret 2 = E, string 3 open = G, string 2 fret 1 = C, string 1 open = E).

exercises.idea: C major is C _ G (E).
Which note is the fifth of C major: E, F or G? (G)
Match the strings of open C to their notes: string 5 / C, string 4 / E, string 3 / G, string 2 / C, string 1 / E.
C major is shown with its root C and fifth G: pick the missing chord tone (E, the third).

lessons.title: Four frets or three
lessons.teaches: A major third is four half steps above the root and a minor third is three, and the third decides whether a chord is major or minor.
facts: A major third is four half steps (four frets) above the root.
A minor third is three half steps (three frets) above the root.
C to E is a major third; C to Eb is a minor third.
The third is the note that makes a chord major or minor.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 5 with C at fret 3, Eb at fret 6 and E at fret 7; audio of C-E then C-Eb.

exercises.idea: From open string 5 (A), tap the major third above on the same string (fret 4, C#).
Two notes: is the second a major third or a minor third above the first?
How many frets is a minor third on one string? (3)

lessons.title: E and Em: one finger apart
lessons.teaches: E major and E minor differ by one note, the third: G# in E, G in Em.
facts: E major is E G# B; E minor is E G B.
Open E (022100) and open Em (022000) differ only on string 3: G# at fret 1 for E, open G for Em.
Lowering the third of a major chord by a half step makes it minor.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord boxes of E (022100) and Em (022000) side by side with the string 3 note labelled 3 or b3 (flat 3, the minor third); audio of both.

exercises.idea: Place open E (022100).
Play E, then lift one finger to play Em.
Is this chord major or minor?

lessons.title: A, Am, D and Dm
lessons.teaches: The same one-note change turns A into Am and D into Dm: the third drops a half step.
facts: Open A (x02220) has C# on string 2 at fret 2; open Am (x02210) has C on string 2 at fret 1.
Open D (xx0232) has F# on string 1 at fret 2; open Dm (xx0231) has F on string 1 at fret 1.
A minor chord is written with a small m after the root: Am, Dm, Em.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord boxes of A (x02220), Am (x02210), D (xx0232) and Dm (xx0231), with the third labelled: string 2 at fret 2 (C#) or fret 1 (C) for A and Am, string 1 at fret 2 (F#) or fret 1 (F) for D and Dm; audio pairs.

exercises.idea: Place Am (x02210).
Place Dm (xx0231).
In open A (x02220), tap the note that you lower to make Am (string 2, fret 2).
Play D, then Dm.

lessons.title: Hearing major and minor
lessons.teaches: A major triad stacks a major third and then a minor third, a minor triad the other way round, and you can hear the difference.
facts: Major chords are usually described as bright and minor chords as darker or sadder.
A major triad is a major third with a minor third on top: C-E-G.
A minor triad is a minor third with a major third on top: A-C-E.
Major and minor triads both have a perfect fifth, seven half steps, from root to fifth.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Audio: pairs of open chords, E (022100) and Em (022000), A (x02220) and Am (x02210), D (xx0232) and Dm (xx0231), then the same chords in random order. Figure: the chord boxes with the third labelled 3 or b3, and C-E-G and A-C-E on string 5 (frets 3, 7, 10 and 0, 3, 7) with the thirds marked.

exercises.idea: Hear a chord: major or minor?
The notes A C E make which chord: A, Am or C? (Am)
A minor triad has a minor third on top of a major third (false).

lessons.title: Power chords: neither major nor minor
lessons.teaches: A power chord is a root and a fifth with no third, so it is neither major nor minor.
facts: A power chord has only the root and the fifth, often with the root doubled an octave up.
With no third, a power chord is neither major nor minor.
Power chords are written with a 5: G5 is G and D.
With the root on string 6 at fret n, the fifth is on string 5 at fret n + 2 and the octave on string 4 at fret n + 2.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab and chord box of G5 (355xxx: string 6 fret 3, strings 5 and 4 fret 5) and the same shape moved to A5 (577xxx); audio.

exercises.idea: Place G5 (string 6 fret 3, string 5 fret 5, string 4 fret 5).
Tap the three notes of A5 with its root on string 6 (frets 5, 7, 7).
G5 is a minor chord (false).
Play E5 using open string 6 (022xxx).

units.checkpoint: Chord, root and triad; the six-character shape spelling (022000, x32010); reading a chord box (strings, frets, nut, o, x and finger numbers); root, third and fifth by counting letters; the major third (4 frets) versus the minor third (3 frets); the differences between E/Em, A/Am and D/Dm; hearing major versus minor; power chords as root and fifth.

units.title: Rhythm for strumming
units.summary: Dotted notes, ties, 3/4 time and time signatures, pickup notes, sixteenth notes, chord changes in time, accents and muted strums.
units.whyItMatters: These are the rhythms behind nearly every strummed song you will want to play.

lessons.title: Dotted notes
lessons.teaches: A dot after a note makes it half as long again.
facts: A dot after a note adds half of the note's own length.
In 4/4 a dotted half note lasts three beats and a dotted quarter note lasts one and a half beats.
A dotted quarter note followed by an eighth note fills two beats.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum Em (022000): dotted half note then a quarter note; then dotted quarter, eighth, half. Figure: rhythm line with counts under each note; audio.

exercises.idea: Tap one bar of 4/4: dotted half note, quarter note.
How many beats does a dotted quarter note last in 4/4? (one and a half)
A dotted half note = half note + _ note (quarter).

lessons.title: Ties
lessons.teaches: A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one longer sound, even across a bar line.
facts: A tie is a curved line joining two notes of the same pitch: play the first and hold it for both lengths.
A tie can carry a note across a bar line, which a dot cannot do.
A curved line joining notes of different pitches is a slur, not a tie.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum Am (x02210) on beat 4 and let it ring, tied over the bar line into beat 1. Figure: rhythm line of two bars with a tie across the bar line; audio.

exercises.idea: Tap two bars where beat 4 of bar 1 is tied to beat 1 of bar 2 (no tap on that beat 1).
You strike a tied note twice (false).
A curve joins a C and a D. Is it a tie or a slur? (a slur)

lessons.title: Three beats in a bar
lessons.teaches: In 3/4 time there are three beats in each bar, with the strongest on beat 1.
facts: In 3/4 time each bar has three beats, with the strongest on beat 1.
The waltz is a dance in 3/4.
A dotted half note fills a whole bar of 3/4.
In a time signature such as 3/4 or 4/4, the top number is the number of beats in a bar and the bottom number 4 means each beat is a quarter note.
lessons.onTheGuitar: On Am (x02210): pick open string 5 on beat 1, strum strings 4 to 1 on beats 2 and 3 ("bass, strum, strum"). Figure: rhythm line of two 3/4 bars; audio.

exercises.idea: Tap two bars of 3/4 with the accent on each beat 1.
Is this music counted in 3 or in 4?
Which single note fills a bar of 3/4? (a dotted half note)

lessons.title: Pickup notes: starting before beat 1
lessons.teaches: Some tunes start with a few pickup notes before the first full bar, so you count the missing beats silently and land on beat 1.
facts: Notes that come before the first full bar are called a pickup (or an anacrusis).
"When the Saints Go Marching In" starts with three pickup notes on beats 2, 3 and 4 ("Oh when the"), and "Saints" lands on beat 1.
"My Bonnie Lies over the Ocean", in 3/4, starts with one pickup note on beat 3 ("My").
Written music often shortens the last bar by the length of the pickup, so the two together make one full bar.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Count "1 2 3 4" and play the pickup of "When the Saints" (traditional) in C on beats 2, 3 and 4: string 2 fret 1 (C), open string 1 (E), string 1 fret 1 (F), then string 1 fret 3 (G) on beat 1, held. Figure: tab and rhythm line with the pickup bar shaded; audio with a count-in.

exercises.idea: After a count-in, tap the opening of "When the Saints": beats 2, 3 and 4, then a long note on beat 1.
Play the pickup and first note of "When the Saints": string 2 fret 1, open string 1, string 1 fret 1, then string 1 fret 3 on beat 1.
In "When the Saints", on which beat does "Saints" land? (beat 1)
Does this tune start on beat 1 or with a pickup?

lessons.title: Sixteenth notes
lessons.teaches: Four sixteenth notes fit in one quarter-note beat, counted "1 e & a".
facts: Four sixteenth notes last as long as one quarter note.
Sixteenth notes are counted 1 e & a 2 e & a 3 e & a 4 e & a.
Sixteenth notes have two flags, or two beams when grouped.
In sixteenth-note strumming the hand goes down on the numbers and "&"s and up on the "e"s and "a"s.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum the muted strings (fretting hand resting flat across them around frets 1 to 3) on every sixteenth note at 60 BPM, down on 1 and &, up on e and a; then the same on Em (022000). Figure: rhythm line of one beat of sixteenths with counts and arrows; audio.

exercises.idea: Tap one beat of four sixteenth notes, then three quarter notes, at 60 BPM.
Count: 1 e _ a 2 _ & a (&, e).
How many sixteenth notes fill a bar of 4/4? (16)

lessons.title: Changing chords in time
lessons.teaches: Chord changes land on beat 1 of the bar, and a chart tells you how many beats each chord lasts.
facts: Unless the chart says otherwise, change to the next chord on beat 1 of the bar.
The last upstroke before a change may hit the open strings, which buys your fretting hand time to move.
In a slash chart each beat gets a mark: the chord symbol on the beat where the chord starts and a slash (/) on each beat after it, as in "| Em / / / |".
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play Em (022000) for one bar and Am (x02210) for one bar with the pattern down, down-up, up, down-up, changing on beat 1: fingers 2 and 3 move over one string (from strings 5 and 4 to strings 4 and 3) and finger 1 joins on string 2 fret 1. Figure: chord chart "| Em / / / | Am / / / |" with chord boxes; audio at 70 BPM.

exercises.idea: Play Em, then Am, changing on beat 1 (Em 022000, Am x02210).
In "| Em / Am / |", on which beat does Am start? (beat 3)
Tap the strumming pattern for two bars without stopping at the bar line.

lessons.title: Accents and muted strums
lessons.teaches: Accents and muted strums shape a strumming pattern, and stressing beats 2 and 4 gives the backbeat.
facts: An accent mark (>) over a note means play it louder than the notes around it.
A muted strum, written as an x note head, is a percussive "chick" made by strumming while the fretting hand rests lightly on the strings.
Stressing beats 2 and 4 is called the backbeat, the feel behind much pop and rock.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum E (022100): down on 1, a muted strum on 2 (lay the fretting fingers flat across all six strings, so the open strings are silenced too), down-up on 3, a muted strum on 4; start at 60 BPM, because the hand leaves and re-forms the chord each time. Figure: rhythm line with x note heads on beats 2 and 4 and accent marks; audio.

exercises.idea: Hear a bar of strumming: which beat is accented?
A muted strum is played with the fretting hand pressing a chord firmly (false).
The backbeat stresses which beats in 4/4? (2 and 4)

units.checkpoint: A dot adds half; lengths of dotted half and dotted quarter notes; ties versus slurs; 3/4 time and what the two numbers of a time signature mean; pickup notes before beat 1; sixteenth notes counted 1 e & a; reading a one-bar pattern and changing chords on beat 1; accents, muted strums and the backbeat on beats 2 and 4.

units.title: Intervals: measuring distance
units.summary: Name the distance between two notes, from the half step to the octave, and hear the common ones.
units.whyItMatters: Intervals are the building blocks of every scale, chord and melody, and the neck is a map of them.

lessons.title: What an interval is
lessons.teaches: An interval is the distance between two notes, numbered by counting letter names from the lower note, counting both ends.
facts: An interval is the distance in pitch between two notes.
An interval's number comes from counting letter names from the lower note to the upper, counting both: C to E is a third (C D E).
Notes played one after the other make a melodic interval; played together, a harmonic interval.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 5 with C (fret 3) and the letters D E F G above it numbered 2 to 5; audio of C-G melodic, then together.

exercises.idea: C to G is which interval number: third, fourth or fifth? (fifth)
C to E is a second (false).
Was the interval melodic (one note after the other) or harmonic (together)?

lessons.title: Seconds and thirds
lessons.teaches: A minor second is one half step, a major second two, a minor third three and a major third four.
facts: A minor second (m2) is one half step; a major second (M2) is two.
A minor third (m3) is three half steps; a major third (M3) is four.
On one string, m2 = 1 fret, M2 = 2 frets, m3 = 3 frets and M3 = 4 frets.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 6 from G (fret 3) with Ab (4), A (5), Bb (6) and B (7) labelled m2, M2, m3, M3.

exercises.idea: Match each interval to its size: m2 / 1, M2 / 2, m3 / 3, M3 / 4 half steps.
From G on string 6 (fret 3), tap the major third on the same string (fret 7, B).
D to F: which interval? (minor third)

lessons.title: Fourths, fifths and octaves
lessons.teaches: A perfect fourth is five half steps, a perfect fifth seven and an octave twelve, and the open strings are mostly fourths apart.
facts: A perfect fourth (P4) is five half steps, a perfect fifth (P5) seven and a perfect octave (P8) twelve.
The perfect intervals are the perfect unison, fourth, fifth and octave (P1, P4, P5, P8).
Neighbouring open strings are a perfect fourth apart, except strings 3 and 2 (G to B), a major third apart.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 6 fret 5 (A2) with the P4 on string 5 at fret 5 (D3) and the P5 on string 5 at fret 7 (E3); open strings labelled with the interval between each pair.

exercises.idea: From A on string 6 (fret 5), tap the perfect fifth on string 5 (fret 7, E).
Match: P4 / 5, P5 / 7, P8 / 12 half steps.
Which pair of neighbouring open strings is not a perfect fourth apart? (G and B)

lessons.title: Sixths and sevenths
lessons.teaches: A minor sixth is eight half steps, a major sixth nine, a minor seventh ten and a major seventh eleven.
facts: A minor sixth (m6) is eight half steps; a major sixth (M6) is nine.
A minor seventh (m7) is ten half steps; a major seventh (M7) is eleven, one half step below the octave.
C to A is a major sixth; C to Bb is a minor seventh; C to B is a major seventh.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 5 from C (fret 3) to frets 11 (Ab, m6), 12 (A, M6), 13 (Bb, m7) and 14 (B, M7); audio of each against C.

exercises.idea: Match: m6 / 8, M6 / 9, m7 / 10, M7 / 11 half steps.
C to Bb is which interval? (minor seventh)
Is this interval a major seventh or an octave?

lessons.title: The tritone
lessons.teaches: Six half steps, exactly half an octave, is the tritone, spelled as an augmented fourth or a diminished fifth.
facts: The interval of six half steps, exactly half an octave, is called the tritone.
Spelled as a fourth it is an augmented fourth (A4, C to F#); spelled as a fifth it is a diminished fifth (d5, C to Gb).
The tritone sounds tense and restless.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: open string 5 (A) and string 5 fret 6 (D# or Eb); string 6 fret 5 (A) with string 5 fret 6 (D#) as a two-string shape; audio.

exercises.idea: From open string 5 (A), tap the tritone on string 5 (fret 6).
Tritone or perfect fifth?
A tritone is seven half steps (false).

lessons.title: Hearing intervals with tunes you know
lessons.teaches: You can recognise an interval by remembering a familiar tune that starts with it.
facts: In "Twinkle Twinkle Little Star" the leap from the second note to the third is a perfect fifth up.
"Frere Jacques" starts with a major second up.
"When the Saints Go Marching In" starts with a major third up.
"Here Comes the Bride" (Wagner's Bridal Chorus) starts with a perfect fourth up.
"My Bonnie Lies over the Ocean" starts with a major sixth up.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Audio: each tune's opening (traditional or public domain) played on guitar, then the bare interval. Figure: the interval as frets on string 5 from A.

exercises.idea: Hear an interval and choose the tune that starts with it.
Match each tune to its opening interval (Twinkle / P5, Frere Jacques / M2, Saints / M3, Bridal Chorus / P4, My Bonnie / M6).
Hear an interval and name it: P4, P5, M3 or M6.

lessons.title: Intervals inside chords
lessons.teaches: Chords are intervals stacked on a root: a major triad is 1 3 5, a minor triad 1 b3 5 and a power chord 1 5.
facts: A major triad is the root, a major third and a perfect fifth above it: 1 3 5.
A minor triad is the root, a minor third and a perfect fifth above it: 1 b3 5.
In chord formulas, 3 means a major third above the root and b3 a minor third.
A power chord is 1 5: a root and a perfect fifth.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord boxes of A (x02220) and Am (x02210) with dots labelled 1, 3 or b3, and 5.

exercises.idea: Open Am is shown with string 2 left empty; name the note that completes the chord (C, the b3).
Which formula is a minor triad: 1 3 5, 1 b3 5 or 1 5? (1 b3 5)
A dot is shown on string 4, fret 2, inside an open A chord; name its interval from the root (5).

units.checkpoint: Interval numbers by counting letters; the half-step size of every interval from m2 to P8, including the tritone; perfect versus major and minor intervals; the intervals between the open strings; recognising P4, P5, M2, M3 and M6 by ear; triads as intervals from the root.

units.title: The major scale
units.summary: The step pattern behind the major scale, scale degrees, spelling major scales, and a movable one-octave shape.
units.whyItMatters: The major scale is the measuring stick for keys, chords, modes and almost everything else in theory.

lessons.title: Whole, whole, half
lessons.teaches: The major scale follows the step pattern whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.
facts: The major scale follows the step pattern W W H W W W H (W = whole step, H = half step).
C major uses only the natural notes: C D E F G A B C.
In C major the half steps fall between E-F and B-C, which are scale steps 3-4 and 7-8.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: C major along string 5 at frets 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15 with W and H marked between the dots; audio ascending.

exercises.idea: Complete the major pattern: W W _ W W W _ (H, H).
Play C major along string 5: frets 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15.
Between which steps of the major scale is the first half step? (3 and 4)

lessons.title: Scale degrees
lessons.teaches: The notes of a scale are numbered 1 to 7 from the tonic; these numbers are its degrees.
facts: The notes of a scale are numbered 1 to 7 from the tonic; these numbers are called scale degrees.
Degree 8 is the tonic again, an octave higher, so it is called 1 again.
Singers name the major-scale degrees do re mi fa sol la ti (do).
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the string 5 C major line with each dot labelled with its degree number and degree colour.

exercises.idea: Which note is degree 5 of C major? (G)
Match degrees to syllables: 1 / do, 3 / mi, 5 / sol, 7 / ti.
A dot is shown on string 5, fret 12, in the C major line; name its degree (6).

lessons.title: G major and its F#
lessons.teaches: Starting the step pattern on G needs one sharp, F#, so that the half step falls between degrees 7 and 8.
facts: G major is G A B C D E F# G.
G major needs F# rather than F to keep a half step between degrees 7 and 8.
A major scale uses each letter name exactly once, so the seventh note of G major is called F#, not Gb.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: G major along string 6 at frets 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, with F# (fret 14) highlighted; audio.

exercises.idea: Complete G major: G A B C D E _ G (F#).
Why is degree 7 of G major called F# and not Gb? (each letter once: G already appears)
Play G major along string 6 from fret 3 to fret 15.

lessons.title: Building any major scale
lessons.teaches: Write the seven letters from the tonic, then add sharps or flats until the steps follow W W H W W W H.
facts: To spell a major scale, write the seven letters starting on the tonic, then add sharps or flats so the steps follow W W H W W W H.
D major is D E F# G A B C# D.
F major is F G A Bb C D E F.
A major scale never mixes sharps and flats: it uses one kind or the other.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: D major and F major each drawn along string 5 from their tonic (D at fret 5, F at fret 8) with the accidentals labelled.

exercises.idea: Type the seventh note of A major (G#).
Complete F major: F G A _ C D E F (Bb).
Which is D major: D E F G A B C, or D E F# G A B C#? (the second)

lessons.title: The major scale in one position
lessons.teaches: One octave of the major scale from a root on string 6 fits under the hand as a movable shape.
facts: One octave of G major from string 6 fret 3: string 6 frets 3, 5; string 5 frets 2, 3, 5; string 4 frets 2, 4, 5.
The shape is movable: start it at string 6 fret 5 and it plays A major.
With one finger per fret, the hand covers frets 2 to 5 for G major, with the second finger on the root.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard frets 1 to 6 with the G major octave (6: 3, 5; 5: 2, 3, 5; 4: 2, 4, 5), finger numbers and degree labels; tab; audio.

exercises.idea: Play one octave of G major from string 6 fret 3, up and back down.
Tap the eight notes of the same shape starting on A (string 6 fret 5).
Starting the shape at string 6 fret 8 gives which major scale? (C)

lessons.title: How the major scale sounds
lessons.teaches: The major scale sounds bright and settled, and its seventh degree pulls strongly up to the tonic.
facts: The major scale is usually heard as bright and settled.
Degree 7, a half step below the tonic, pulls strongly up to it; it is called the leading tone.
Many traditional melodies, such as "Twinkle Twinkle Little Star" and "Frere Jacques", use only the notes of a major scale.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Audio: G major up to degree 7 and stopping there (unresolved), then resolving to G. Figure: the one-octave shape with degree 7 (string 4 fret 4, F#) highlighted.

exercises.idea: Hear a scale: is it the major scale or the minor pentatonic?
Does this melody end on the tonic or leave you hanging?
The leading tone is degree 2 of the scale (false).

lessons.title: Major pentatonic: the major scale minus two
lessons.teaches: The major pentatonic scale is the major scale without degrees 4 and 7: 1 2 3 5 6.
facts: The major pentatonic scale is the major scale without degrees 4 and 7: 1 2 3 5 6.
C major pentatonic is C D E G A.
C major pentatonic and A minor pentatonic contain the same five notes; they differ in which note is home.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 5 with C major pentatonic (C 3, D 5, E 7, G 10, A 12) and the A minor pentatonic box 1 with its C notes ringed; audio of both scales, each over its own drone.

exercises.idea: Complete C major pentatonic: C D _ G _ (E, A).
Which two degrees of the major scale does major pentatonic leave out? (4 and 7)
Same five notes over two drones: which sounds major?

units.checkpoint: The pattern W W H W W W H; scale degrees 1 to 7 and do re mi; spelling C, G, D, F and A major with each letter once; the one-octave shape from string 6 and how moving it changes the key; the leading tone; major pentatonic as 1 2 3 5 6 and its link to the minor pentatonic with the same notes.

units.title: Chords that belong together
units.summary: What a key is, the seven chords of a major key, roman numerals, and the progressions built from them.
units.whyItMatters: This is why G, C, D and Em sound good together, and how you can work out the chords of any song in a major key.

lessons.title: What a key is
lessons.teaches: A piece is in a key when its notes come mainly from one scale and it feels at home on that scale's tonic.
facts: A piece is in a key when its notes come mainly from one scale and it feels at home on that scale's tonic.
Music in the key of G major uses the notes of the G major scale and feels at home on G.
The chord built on the tonic is the home chord; many songs end on it.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Audio: a short progression in G (G, C, D, G) and the same chords ending on D. Figure: chord boxes of G (320003), C (x32010) and D (xx0232).

exercises.idea: Two endings: which one finishes on the home chord?
A song uses mainly the notes G A B C D E F# and ends on G. Which key is it in? (G major)
A key is a single note (false).

lessons.title: Stacking thirds in the scale
lessons.teaches: Building a triad on each degree from every other note of the scale gives the seven chords of the key.
facts: Building a triad on each scale degree from every other note of the scale gives the chords of the key.
In C major the triads are C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am and Bdim.
Chords built only from a key's scale are called diatonic chords.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the C major scale with triads stacked on each degree (C E G, D F A, E G B, F A C, G B D, A C E, B D F); chord boxes of C, Dm, Em, F (small F, xx3211), G and Am; audio.

exercises.idea: The triad on D in C major is D _ A (F).
Which triad is built on degree 5 of C major? (G: G B D)
Place Dm (xx0231), the chord on degree 2 of C major.

lessons.title: Major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished
lessons.teaches: In every major key the seven triads follow the same qualities: major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.
facts: In every major key the triads are, from degree 1 to 7: major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.
A diminished triad is a minor third with another minor third on top: B D F in C major.
In G major the chords are G, Am, Bm, C, D, Em and F#dim.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord boxes for the open chords of G major (G 320003, Am x02210, Bm x24432, a barre chord you will learn later, C x32010, D xx0232, Em 022000), and F#dim as a three-string triad (xx421x: F# A C on strings 4 to 2), each labelled with its quality.

exercises.idea: Which degree of a major key has the diminished triad? (7)
The chords of D major: D, Em, _, G, A, Bm, C#dim (F#m).
Degree 4 of a major key has a minor chord (false).

lessons.title: Roman numerals
lessons.teaches: Roman numerals name chords by their scale degree, with upper case for major, lower case for minor and ° for diminished.
facts: Roman numerals name chords by scale degree: I ii iii IV V vi vii°.
Upper case means a major chord, lower case a minor chord, and ° a diminished chord.
Roman numerals describe a progression in any key: I-IV-V is C-F-G in C and G-C-D in G.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: a table of the seven numerals over the chords of C and of G, with chord boxes for the open shapes.

exercises.idea: Match numerals to chords in C: I / C, ii / Dm, IV / F, V / G, vi / Am.
In G major, which chord is IV? (C)
Why is vi written in lower case? (it is a minor chord)

lessons.title: I, IV and V
lessons.teaches: I, IV and V are the three major chords of a major key, and together they can accompany a huge number of songs.
facts: I, IV and V are the three major chords of a major key.
I-IV-V in guitar-friendly keys: G-C-D, D-G-A, A-D-E, E-A-B and C-F-G.
A huge number of folk, blues, rock and country songs use only I, IV and V.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play G (320003), C (x32010) and D (xx0232) four beats each, then the same I-IV-V in A: A (x02220), D, E (022100). Figure: chord boxes with I, IV and V labels; audio.

exercises.idea: Play I-IV-V-I in G: G, C, D, G.
What is V in the key of A? (E)
I-IV-V in D: D, _, A (G).

lessons.title: Adding vi
lessons.teaches: The vi chord is the minor chord on degree 6, and with I, IV and V it makes the most common progressions in pop.
facts: The vi chord is the minor chord built on degree 6: Am in C, Em in G.
The progression I-V-vi-IV (in G: G-D-Em-C) is one of the most used in pop music.
I and vi share two notes (C E G and A C E share C and E), so they sound closely related.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play G, D, Em (022000), C, one bar each, with the strumming pattern from earlier. Figure: chord boxes with numerals; audio of I-V-vi-IV and I-vi-IV-V.

exercises.idea: Play I-V-vi-IV in G: G, D, Em, C.
Which progression did you hear: I-IV-V-I or I-V-vi-IV?
Which chord is vi in D major? (Bm)

units.checkpoint: What a key is; diatonic triads by stacking every other scale note; the pattern major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished; roman numerals and their upper and lower case; I-IV-V and I-V-vi-IV in G, C, D, A and E; naming the chords of a key with up to two sharps or one flat.

units.title: Reading music: the staff
units.summary: The staff, the treble clef, how guitar music is written an octave up, the open strings on the staff, and first reading on strings 1 to 3.
units.whyItMatters: Standard notation opens up method books, classical guitar and any music written for other instruments.

lessons.title: Five lines, four spaces
lessons.teaches: Standard notation writes notes on a staff of five lines and four spaces, and higher notes sit higher.
facts: Standard notation writes notes on a staff of five lines and four spaces.
The higher a note sits on the staff, the higher it sounds.
A note sits either on a line (the line runs through its head) or in a space.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: an empty staff with lines and spaces numbered from the bottom, then two notes, one higher than the other, each joined to the string that plays it (open string 3 for the lower, open string 1 for the higher), so higher on the staff is higher on the guitar; audio.

exercises.idea: Two notes are shown; which one is higher? (the one placed higher)
A staff has four lines and five spaces (false).
Is the shown note on a line or in a space?
Two notes are shown on the staff and one is played: which one did you hear, the higher or the lower?

lessons.title: The treble clef
lessons.teaches: Guitar music uses the treble clef, whose lines are E G B D F and spaces F A C E from the bottom.
facts: Guitar music is written in the treble clef, also called the G clef because its curl circles the G line (the second line from the bottom).
The lines of the treble staff, bottom to top, are E G B D F; the spaces are F A C E.
A memory sentence for the lines from the bottom: Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: treble staff with each line and space labelled; tapping one plays its sound and lights where it is played in first position (the E on the bottom line at string 4 fret 2, the F on the top line at string 1 fret 1).

exercises.idea: Name the note on the middle line (B).
Place F on the staff (the bottom space or the top line).
Treble clef spaces from the bottom: F _ C _ (A, E).

lessons.title: Guitar sounds an octave lower
lessons.teaches: Guitar music is written one octave higher than it sounds, so it fits on the treble staff.
facts: Guitar music is written one octave higher than it sounds, so that it fits on the treble staff.
A treble clef with a small 8 below it shows this shift; guitar music with a plain treble clef is read the same way.
In first position, the C written in the third space is played at string 2 fret 1 and sounds C4, the piano's middle C.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the written C in the third space beside string 2 fret 1 on a fretboard, with a keyboard showing the sounding C4; audio.

exercises.idea: A guitar sounds an octave higher than written (false).
Where do you play the C written in the third space: string 2 fret 1 or string 5 fret 3? (string 2 fret 1)
Name the note in the third space (C).

lessons.title: The open strings on the staff
lessons.teaches: Strings 1, 2, 3 and 4 open are written in the top space, on the middle line, on the second line and just below the staff.
facts: Open string 1 (high E) is written in the top space of the staff.
Open string 2 (B) is written on the middle line; open string 3 (G) on the second line from the bottom.
Open string 4 (D) is written in the space just below the bottom line.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: staff with written E5, B4, G4, D4 joined to open strings 1, 2, 3, 4 on a fretboard; audio of each.

exercises.idea: Match each written note to its open string: top space / 1, middle line / 2, second line / 3, space below / 4.
Name the note written on the second line (G).
Read the written note (an open string) and play it.

lessons.title: Ledger lines and the low strings
lessons.teaches: Ledger lines extend the staff; the low open strings A and E are written two and three ledger lines below it.
facts: Ledger lines are short extra lines that extend the staff above or below.
Open string 5 (A) is written on the second ledger line below the staff.
Open string 6 (low E) is written just below the third ledger line under the staff.
In first position, the C written on one ledger line below the staff is played at string 5 fret 3; it sounds an octave below the piano's middle C.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: staff with written C4 (one ledger line), A3 (two) and E3 (below three) beside string 5 fret 3, open string 5 and open string 6.

exercises.idea: Name the note on the second ledger line below the staff (A).
Place the written note for open string 6 (E below three ledger lines).
The C on one ledger line below the staff is played where? (string 5, fret 3)

lessons.title: Reading on strings 1 to 3
lessons.teaches: In first position the natural notes on strings 1 to 3 are G and A on string 3, B, C and D on string 2, and E, F and G on string 1.
facts: In first position each finger takes one fret: finger 1 on fret 1 up to finger 4 on fret 4.
First-position naturals: string 3 G (open) and A (2); string 2 B (open), C (1) and D (3); string 1 E (open), F (1) and G (3).
In first position the finger number matches the fret number: C on string 2 fret 1 uses finger 1.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: staff from written G4 to G5 above a fretboard of strings 1 to 3, frets 0 to 4, each note linked to its fret; an original eight-bar quarter-note melody on these notes; audio.

exercises.idea: Name the written note on the fourth line (D).
Read and play a short melody in quarter notes on strings 1 to 3.
The written F on the top line: tap where you play it in first position (string 1, fret 1).
Tap where the written D on the fourth line is played in first position (string 2, fret 3).

units.checkpoint: Five lines and four spaces; treble-clef lines E G B D F and spaces F A C E; guitar sounds an octave below where it is written; where each open string is written (string 6 below three ledger lines, string 5 on the second ledger line below, string 4 in the space below, strings 3, 2, 1 on the second line, middle line and top space); first-position natural notes on strings 1 to 3; reading a short melody.

stages.title: Intermediate: the whole neck and how harmony works

units.title: Intervals: quality, spelling and shapes
units.summary: Full interval names, spelling by letters, inversions, interval shapes on the neck, compound intervals and consonance.
units.whyItMatters: Seeing intervals as shapes lets you build any chord or melody anywhere on the neck without memorising positions.

lessons.title: Perfect, major, minor, augmented, diminished
lessons.teaches: An interval's full name is a quality plus a number, and only some numbers can be major and minor.
facts: An interval's full name is its quality plus its number: major third, perfect fifth.
Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths can be major or minor; unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves can be perfect but never major or minor.
Widening a major or perfect interval by a half step, keeping its letters, makes it augmented.
Narrowing a minor or perfect interval by a half step, keeping its letters, makes it diminished.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 5 from C (fret 3) with G (fret 10, P5), G# (fret 11, A5) and Gb (fret 9, d5) labelled.

exercises.idea: Which of these can be perfect: a third, a fifth or a sixth? (a fifth)
C to G# is a what? (augmented fifth)
A fourth can be major (false).

lessons.title: The spelling decides the name
lessons.teaches: Two intervals can sound the same yet have different names, because the number comes from the letters.
facts: C to D# is an augmented second and C to Eb is a minor third, though both are three half steps.
Intervals that sound the same but are spelled differently are called enharmonic intervals.
Use the spelling that gives the right number: the major third above B is D#, not Eb.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: one fret position on string 5 (fret 6) labelled both D# and Eb, with the C at fret 3; the two names shown with their letter counts (C D = 2, C D E = 3).

exercises.idea: Type the note a major third above B (D#).
E to G#: major third or diminished fourth? (major third)
Type the note a minor third above F# (A).

lessons.title: Turning intervals upside down
lessons.teaches: Inverting an interval moves one note an octave, and the two intervals always add up to nine with qualities swapped.
