Which bass note is under the D chord: D, F# or C?

lessons.title: Bass lines with slash chords
lessons.teaches: Slash chords let the bass move by step while the chords change, the classic descending line C, C/B, Am, Am/G.
facts: Slash chords let the bass walk step by step while the harmony changes: C, C/B, Am, Am/G.
C/B contains B, the major 7th of C, so it can also be named Cmaj7/B.
On guitar, slash chords often keep a familiar shape and change only the lowest note.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play C (x32010), C/B (x22010), Am (x02210), Am/G (3x2210), F (xx3211), each two beats. Figure: chord boxes with the bass line C B A G F shown as a line on strings 5 and 6; audio.

exercises.idea: Play C, C/B, Am, Am/G.
Order the chords so the bass falls by step: Am, C/B, Am/G, C (C, C/B, Am, Am/G).
Does the bass line fall or rise?

lessons.title: Pedal points
lessons.teaches: A pedal point is one note, usually in the bass, held or repeated while the chords above it change.
facts: A pedal point is one note, usually in the bass, held or repeated while the chords above it change.
Open strings make easy pedals on guitar: chords moving above open string 5 (A) or open string 4 (D).
Moving between D, Dsus4 and Dsus2 over the open D string is a classic guitar pedal figure.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab of an original figure: open string 4 under D (xx0232), Dsus4 (xx0233), D, Dsus2 (xx0230), and A, Asus4, A, Asus2 over open string 5; audio.

exercises.idea: Play D, Dsus4, D, Dsus2 keeping the open D string ringing.
In a pedal point the bass note changes with every chord (false).
Is the bass note held (a pedal) or moving?

units.checkpoint: sus2 and sus4 (no 3rd), the sus4-to-major resolution and the 7sus4; add9 versus 9; add4; 6, m6 and 6/9 chords and C6 versus Am7; slash chords as inversions or as new bass notes; descending bass lines with slash chords; pedal points on open strings.

units.title: Transposing, the capo and Nashville numbers
units.summary: Moving music to a new key by interval and by numerals, capo arithmetic, choosing a key, and writing progressions as numbers.
units.whyItMatters: With these you can play any song in a key that suits your voice using the chord shapes you already know.

lessons.title: Transposing
lessons.teaches: To transpose is to move every note or chord of a piece by the same interval into a new key, and writing the chords as numerals first makes it easy.
facts: To transpose is to move music to a new key by moving every note or chord by the same interval.
C Am F G transposed up a whole step is D Bm G A.
Chord qualities never change when you transpose: minor stays minor and a 7 stays a 7.
Writing the chords as roman numerals first, then reading them in the new key, keeps every chord right: I-V-vi-IV is G D Em C in G and A E F#m D in A.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: C (x32010), Am (x02210), F (xx3211), G (320003) and beside them D (xx0232), Bm (x24432), G (320003), A (x02220), with an arrow labelled "up a whole step" and the numerals I vi IV V under both; audio of both.

exercises.idea: Transpose Em7 up a perfect fourth (Am7).
G C D up a whole step: A _ E (D).
Transposing can turn a minor chord into a major chord (false).
Two progressions are played: is the second the same progression in a new key?
I-vi-IV-V in D: D, Bm, G, _ (A).

lessons.title: How a capo works
lessons.teaches: A capo raises every open string by the number of frets it sits at, so the same shapes sound higher.
facts: A capo clamps across the strings at a fret and raises every open string by that many half steps.
Chords are named by shape when you use a capo, but they sound higher: a G shape with a capo at fret 2 sounds A.
Tab for capo songs usually counts frets from the capo, so 0 means the capo fret.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: neck with a capo at fret 2 and a G shape behind it, labelled "shape G, sounds A"; audio of G open, then with the capo.

exercises.idea: An E shape with a capo at fret 3 sounds which chord? (G)
In most capo tab, with the capo at fret 2, a 0 means the open string behind the capo (false: it means the capo fret).
With a capo at fret 2, play the G shape; it sounds A.
The same G shape is strummed twice: which time was the capo on (the higher-sounding one)?

lessons.title: Capo arithmetic
lessons.teaches: Sounding chord equals shape plus capo; to use easy shapes in a hard key, subtract the capo from the key.
facts: Sounding chord = shape + capo fret in half steps: a C shape with capo 3 sounds Eb.
To play a key with easy shapes, subtract: for Bb using G shapes, put the capo at fret 3.
A song with Bb, Eb, F and Gm can be played with G, C, D and Em shapes and the capo at fret 3.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: a two-column table, sounding chords (Bb Eb F Gm) and capo-3 shapes (G C D Em), with chord boxes; audio.

exercises.idea: Capo at fret 5, D shape: which chord sounds? (G)
To play in A with G shapes, where does the capo go? (fret 2)
A song in E with capo 4 can use the shapes of _ major (C).

lessons.title: Choosing a key to sing in
lessons.teaches: Move a song down if it is too high to sing and up if it is too low, then choose a capo position that keeps easy shapes.
facts: If a song sits too high for your voice, transpose it down; too low, transpose it up.
Two guitars can play one song in different shapes for a fuller sound: open G shapes and D shapes with capo 5 both sound in G.
After transposing, look for a capo position that turns the new chords into open shapes.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the same I-IV-V in G as open G C D, and as D G A shapes with a capo at fret 5; audio of both guitars together.

exercises.idea: A song in G is too high for you by a whole step. Which key do you try? (F)
With D shapes, where does the capo go to sound in E? (fret 2)
G shapes in open position and C shapes with capo 7 both sound in G (true).

lessons.title: The Nashville number system
lessons.teaches: The Nashville number system writes chords as numbers of the key, so one chart works in any key.
facts: The Nashville number system writes chords as numbers of the key: 1 4 5 in G is G C D.
A minor chord gets a minus sign or a small m: 6- (or 6m) is Em in G.
A slash number marks the bass: 1/3 in C is C/E.
A number chart works in any key; the band only needs to be told the key.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: an original number chart (1 | 5 | 6- | 4 | 1/3 | 4 | 5 | 1) read in G (G 320003, D xx0232, Em 022000, C x32010, G/B x20003) and then in D (D xx0232, A x02220, Bm x24432, G 320003, D/F# 2x0232); audio.

exercises.idea: In D, the chart 1 4 6- 5 is D G _ A (Bm).
Write E minor in the key of G as a number (6-).
In C, what is 5/7? (G/B)

units.checkpoint: Transposing by interval and by numerals with chord qualities kept; how a capo raises pitch and how capo tab counts frets; capo arithmetic both ways (shape plus capo gives the sound; key minus capo gives the shape); two guitars in different capo positions; Nashville numbers with minus signs and slash numbers.

units.title: Improvising: notes that fit
units.summary: Arpeggios, chord tones on strong beats, target notes at chord changes, motifs, and call and response.
units.whyItMatters: These ideas turn running up and down a scale into solos that follow the chords and say something.

lessons.title: Arpeggios
lessons.teaches: An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time, which turns chord tones into a melody.
facts: An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time.
A major arpeggio is 1 3 5 (and 8); a minor arpeggio is 1 b3 5 (and 8).
One octave of A major from string 6 fret 5: string 6 fret 5, string 5 frets 4 and 7, string 4 fret 7; for A minor, the 3rd moves to string 6 fret 8.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard frets 4 to 8 with the A and Am one-octave arpeggios, degrees labelled; tab; audio.

exercises.idea: Play the A major arpeggio from string 6 fret 5 up to string 4 fret 7 and back.
Tap the notes of a C major arpeggio from string 5 fret 3 (string 5 frets 3 and 7, string 4 fret 5, string 3 fret 5).
Major or minor arpeggio?

lessons.title: Seventh-chord arpeggios
lessons.teaches: A seventh arpeggio adds the 7th, and over a chord its own arpeggio gives the most "inside" notes.
facts: A seventh arpeggio adds the 7th to the triad: Am7 is A C E G.
Over a chord, its own arpeggio gives the most stable notes you can play.
A minor pentatonic contains the whole Am7 arpeggio (A C E G) plus D.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: box 1 of A minor pentatonic with A C E G in chord-tone colours and D plain; audio over an Am7 vamp.

exercises.idea: In box 1 of A minor pentatonic, tap every note that is not in Am7 (the Ds).
Type the notes of Dm7 (D F A C).
Over Am7, play the Am7 arpeggio in box 1, then a phrase ending on G.

lessons.title: Chord tones on strong beats
lessons.teaches: Placing chord tones on strong beats and other scale notes between them makes a line outline the chords.
facts: Chord tones (the 1, 3, 5 and 7 of the chord being played) sound stable; other scale notes sound like passing colour.
Placing chord tones on the strong beats (1 and 3 in 4/4) and other notes between them makes a line follow the harmony.
A non-chord tone on a strong beat sounds tense and usually moves by step to a chord tone.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: a two-bar line in fifth position over Am (x02210) to Dm (xx0231), with the beat 1 and 3 notes highlighted as chord tones: A (string 4 fret 7) and C (string 3 fret 5) over Am, D (string 3 fret 7) and F (string 2 fret 6) over Dm; audio over the backing.

exercises.idea: Which line puts chord tones on the strong beats?
Over Dm, which note is a chord tone: E, F or G? (F)
Over Am, play eighth notes in box 1 so that beats 1 and 3 land on A, C or E.

lessons.title: Aiming at the change
lessons.teaches: A target note is a chord tone you aim to land on as the chord changes, and the 3rd is the strongest target.
facts: A target note is a chord tone you aim to land on at the moment the chord changes.
The 3rd is the strongest target because it tells the ear whether the new chord is major or minor.
Over A7 to D7, the 3rd C# moving down a half step to C (the b7 of D7) marks the change clearly.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard around fret 5 with the 3rds of A7 (C#) and D7 (F#) ringed and the C# to C half step shown on string 3 (frets 6 to 5); audio over a blues backing.

exercises.idea: Between frets 2 and 7, tap every F#, the 3rd of D7 (string 6 fret 2, string 4 fret 4, string 2 fret 7, string 1 fret 2).
Over A7 to D7, land on C (string 3 fret 5) on beat 1 of the D7 bar.
Which note best marks a change to E7: E, G# or B? (G#)

lessons.title: Motifs
lessons.teaches: A motif is a short idea that you repeat and develop, which makes a solo sound composed rather than random.
facts: A motif is a short musical idea, a few notes or a rhythm, that is repeated and developed.
Ways to develop a motif: repeat it, move it to other notes (a sequence), change its rhythm, or change its ending.
A solo built from one or two developed motifs sounds composed rather than random.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab of an original three-note motif in box 1, then the motif repeated, sequenced one scale step up and rhythmically varied; audio.

exercises.idea: Play the motif, then a sequence of it starting one note higher in the box.
Was the second phrase a repeat, a sequence or a new idea?
Order the versions as played: original, repeat, sequence, new ending.

lessons.title: Call and response, and space
lessons.teaches: Pairing a phrase with an answer, and leaving rests between phrases, gives a solo shape and makes it easy to follow.
facts: Call and response pairs a phrase (the call) with an answering phrase.
Rests between phrases give the listener time to hear them and give you time to plan the next one.
Ending on a chord tone on a strong beat sounds finished; ending elsewhere invites an answer.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab of an original two-bar call ending on D (string 3 fret 7) and its answer ending on A (string 4 fret 7), with a bar of rest between; audio over Am.

exercises.idea: Hear a two-bar call, then play your own two-bar answer from box 1.
Which ending sounds like a question and which like an answer?
Good solos leave no rests (false).

units.checkpoint: Arpeggios as chord tones played one at a time; major, minor and seventh arpeggio shapes; Am7 inside A minor pentatonic; chord tones on strong beats and stepwise resolution; aiming for the 3rd at a chord change; developing a motif by repetition, sequence and rhythm; call and response and the use of rests.

stages.title: Expert: advanced harmony, improvisation and the physics of sound

units.title: Rhythm: compound and odd meters
units.summary: Simple versus compound time, 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8, odd meters, mixed meter, hemiola and polyrhythm.
units.whyItMatters: Folk jigs, slow blues, progressive rock and much of the world's music live in these meters.

lessons.title: Simple and compound time
lessons.teaches: In simple time each beat divides into two; in compound time each beat divides into three and is a dotted note.
facts: In simple meters each beat divides into two; in compound meters each beat divides into three.
In compound meters the beat is a dotted note: in 6/8 the beat is a dotted quarter note.
The top number of a compound meter counts the divisions, not the beats: 6/8 has six eighth notes but two beats.
Common time (a C) means 4/4; cut time (a C with a vertical line through it) means 2/2, two half-note beats per bar.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Pick open string 5 in a bar of 2/4 with eighth notes (two beats of two), then a bar of 6/8 (two beats of three). Figure: rhythm lines of both bars with beat groupings bracketed; audio.

exercises.idea: How many beats are in a bar of 6/8? (2)
Match: 2/4 / simple duple, 3/4 / simple triple, 6/8 / compound duple, 9/8 / compound triple.
Does each beat divide into two or into three?

lessons.title: 6/8 time
lessons.teaches: 6/8 has two beats of three eighth notes each, which makes it feel different from 3/4 though both hold six eighths.
facts: 6/8 has two beats per bar, each a dotted quarter divided into three eighth notes.
Count 6/8 as "1 2 3 4 5 6" with accents on 1 and 4, or as "1 & a 2 & a".
3/4 and 6/8 both hold six eighth notes, but 3/4 groups them in three pairs (2+2+2) and 6/8 in two threes (3+3).
lessons.onTheGuitar: Arpeggiate Am (x02210) in 6/8, six eighth notes per bar: string 5, string 3, string 2, string 4, string 3, string 2, so the bass notes fall on counts 1 and 4. Figure: rhythm line of 6/8 next to 3/4 with accents; audio.

exercises.idea: Tap one bar of 6/8 eighth notes, accenting 1 and 4.
In 6/8, which note value gets one beat? (the dotted quarter)

lessons.title: 9/8 and 12/8
lessons.teaches: 9/8 has three dotted-quarter beats and 12/8 has four, each divided into three.
facts: 9/8 has three dotted-quarter beats per bar; 12/8 has four.
12/8 is common in slow blues and ballads, where each of the four beats carries a triplet feel.
A shuffle written in 4/4 with swung eighths and one written in 12/8 can sound the same.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum E7 (020100) in 12/8: down on each beat and on the third eighth of each group. Figure: rhythm line of 12/8 beside 4/4 with triplets; audio of a slow blues feel.

exercises.idea: How many beats in a bar of 12/8? (4)
Tap the four beats of a 12/8 bar while the eighths play.
12/8 has twelve beats per bar (false).

lessons.title: Fives and sevens
lessons.teaches: Odd meters such as 5/4 and 7/8 are felt as groups of twos and threes.
facts: Odd meters such as 5/4 and 7/8 cannot be divided into equal groups of two or three, so they are felt as mixed groups of twos and threes.
5/4 is usually felt as 3+2 or 2+3; 7/8 as 2+2+3, 3+2+2 or 2+3+2.
The grouping can be written into the time signature, as in 3+2+2/8.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play an original riff on string 6 in 7/8 grouped 2+2+3, accenting the first note of each group. Figure: rhythm line with the groups bracketed; audio.

exercises.idea: Tap a bar of 7/8 grouped 2+2+3, accenting each group's first note.
Is this bar of 7/8 grouped 2+2+3 or 3+2+2?
How many eighth notes are in a bar of 7/8? (7)

lessons.title: Mixed meter and hemiola
lessons.teaches: Mixed meter changes the time signature from bar to bar, and a hemiola makes two bars of three feel like three bars of two.
facts: Mixed meter changes the time signature from bar to bar.
A hemiola makes two bars of three beats feel like three bars of two beats by accenting every second beat.
Hemiolas are common at cadences in Baroque music and in Latin American styles that move between 6/8 and 3/4.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Strum two bars of 3/4 on Am (x02210) with accents on beats 1 and 3 of bar 1 and beat 2 of bar 2. Figure: two 3/4 bars with the accents and the 3 x 2 regrouping drawn above them; audio.

exercises.idea: Do these two bars feel like two groups of three or three groups of two?
Tap the hemiola accents across two bars of 3/4.
A hemiola changes the tempo (false).

lessons.title: Three against two
lessons.teaches: A polyrhythm plays two even divisions of the same span at once, and 3 against 2 is the most common one.
facts: A polyrhythm plays two different even divisions of the same span at once, such as 3 against 2.
Counted in six, 3 against 2 has the twos on 1 and 4, the threes on 1, 3 and 5, so the combined rhythm falls on 1, 3, 4 and 5.
A guitar thumb in quarter notes against a melody in quarter-note triplets is a 3-against-2 polyrhythm.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Thumb plays open string 6 on beats 1 and 2 of a 2/4 bar while fingers play three triplet quarters on string 1. Figure: two rhythm lines aligned on a six-step grid; audio slow then at tempo.

exercises.idea: Tap the combined 3-against-2 rhythm (1, 3, 4, 5 in six).
Is this 3 against 2 or straight eighths?
In six, the twos fall on 1 and _ (4).

units.checkpoint: Simple versus compound meters and the dotted-note beat; common time and cut time; counting 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 and the difference between 3/4 and 6/8; groupings of 5/4 and 7/8; mixed meter and hemiola; the composite rhythm of 3 against 2.

units.title: Extended chords: 9, 11 and 13
units.summary: Ninth, eleventh and thirteenth chords, which notes to keep and drop, and which extensions belong to a key.
units.whyItMatters: Extensions are the rich colours of jazz, soul, funk and gospel, and they are easy to grab on guitar once you know what to leave out.

lessons.title: Beyond the seventh
lessons.teaches: Extended chords keep stacking thirds above the 7th, adding the 9th, 11th and 13th.
facts: Extended chords keep stacking thirds above the 7th: the 9th, 11th and 13th.
A 9th chord contains a 7th; a chord with a 9th and no 7th is an add9.
The 9th, 11th and 13th are the 2nd, 4th and 6th an octave higher.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: C stacked in thirds on the neck from C3 to A4, each labelled 1 3 5 b7 9 11 13: C (string 5 fret 3), E (string 4 fret 2), G (open string 3), Bb (string 3 fret 3), D (string 2 fret 3), F (string 1 fret 1), A (string 1 fret 5); audio as a rolled chord.

exercises.idea: Which interval is the 13th an octave higher? (the 6th)
Cadd9 or C9: which has a Bb? (C9)
Stacking thirds from C: C E G Bb _ F A (D).

lessons.title: Ninth chords
lessons.teaches: The three main ninth chords are the dominant 9, major 9 and minor 9, each a seventh chord plus the 9th.
facts: C9 is C E G Bb D; Cmaj9 is C E G B D; Cm9 is C Eb G Bb D.
A common C9 shape with the root on string 5 is x32333.
Guitar 9th chords often leave out the 5th so that the 9th fits under four fingers.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord boxes of C9 (x32333), Cmaj9 (x3243x) and Cm9 (x3133x); audio.

exercises.idea: Type the 9th of A9 (B).
Place C9 (x32333).
Dominant 9 or minor 9?

lessons.title: Elevenths: natural and sharp
lessons.teaches: Minor chords take the natural 11 easily, while major and dominant chords usually take the #11 to avoid a clash with the 3rd.
facts: On a major or dominant chord the natural 11 sits a minor ninth above the 3rd (F over E in C) and clashes, so it is usually avoided.
Minor chords take the 11th easily: Am11 is A C E G B D.
On major and dominant chords the usual eleventh is #11: Cmaj7#11 is C E G B F#.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: Am11 (530000: A C D G B E) and Fmaj7#11 without its 5th (xx3200: F A B E, with the #11 on string 2); audio of Cmaj7 with 11 and with #11.

exercises.idea: Cmaj7 with the natural 11 or with #11: which sounds smoother?
Type the 11th of Dm11 (G).
The natural 11 is a common addition to major 7th chords (false).

lessons.title: Thirteenth chords
lessons.teaches: A 13th chord adds the 13th to a dominant 9 chord, usually leaving out the 11th, and on guitar it is played with only four notes.
facts: In practice C13 is C E G Bb D A: the 11th is normally left out.
On guitar a 13th chord is often played as root, b7, 3rd and 13th: G13 = 3x345x.
A chord with a 6th and a b7 is a 13th chord; a 6 chord has no 7th.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord box of G13 (3x345x) with dots labelled 1, b7, 3, 13, beside G7 (3x343x); audio of G7 to G13.

exercises.idea: Place G13 (3x345x).
Which note does G13 add to G7 in the shape 3x345x? (E)
C6 and C13 are the same chord (false).

lessons.title: What to leave out
lessons.teaches: When a chord has more notes than you can play, keep the 3rd and 7th and drop the 5th first, then the root, then lesser extensions.
facts: When a chord has more notes than you can play, drop the 5th first, then the root (especially if a bass player has it), then the less important extensions.
The 3rd and 7th define a chord's quality and are kept.
Root, 3rd, 7th and 13th are enough to sound a 13th chord.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: C13 spelled in full (6 notes) and then reduced to C, Bb, E, A on strings 5, 3, 2, 1 (x3x355); audio of both.

exercises.idea: Which note of a 9th chord is usually dropped first? (the 5th)
Which two notes define a chord's quality? (3rd and 7th)
From C9 (x32333), lift the finger on the 5th (string 1) to play a four-note C9 (x3233x).

lessons.title: Which extensions fit the key
lessons.teaches: Only some extensions stay inside the key: the 9th fits most diatonic chords, but not iii or vii, and IVmaj7 takes a diatonic #11.
facts: In C major, Cmaj9, Dm9, Fmaj9, G9 and Am9 use only notes of the key.
Em9 is not diatonic to C major, because the 9th of E is F#.
Fmaj7#11 is diatonic to C major: the #11 of F is B.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the C major seventh chords with their diatonic 9ths, 11ths and 13ths listed above each, and movable shapes Cmaj9 (x3243x), Dm9 (x5355x) and G9 (x-10-9-10-10-x); outside notes (the F# of Em9) in red with a label; audio.

exercises.idea: In C major, is Dm9 diatonic? (yes)
Type the #11 of Fmaj7#11 (B).
Which C major chord cannot take a natural 9 diatonically: Em7 or Am7? (Em7)

units.checkpoint: 9, 11 and 13 as stacked thirds and as the 2nd, 4th and 6th an octave up; 9 versus add9; spelling 9th chords and a movable shape; why major and dominant chords take #11 and minor chords take 11; how 13th chords are voiced on guitar; which tones to drop first; which extensions are diatonic in a major key.

units.title: Secondary dominants
units.summary: Dominants of chords other than the tonic, how to spot them, chains of dominants and secondary leading-tone chords.
units.whyItMatters: Secondary dominants are the chromatic chords you meet most often, in everything from Bach to ragtime to pop.

lessons.title: The dominant of another chord
lessons.teaches: A secondary dominant is the V or V7 of a chord other than the tonic, which briefly makes that chord sound like home.
facts: A secondary dominant is the V (or V7) of a chord other than the tonic, written V/x or V7/x.
In C major, D7 is V7/V: the V7 of G.
A secondary dominant briefly treats its target chord as a temporary tonic; this is called tonicization.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play C, D7 (xx0212), G, C. Figure: chord boxes with numerals I, V7/V, V, I and the F# in D7 highlighted as outside the key; audio.

exercises.idea: In G major, what is V7/V? (A7)
Was the chord before G a plain ii (Am) or V7/V (D7)?
Type the chord that is V7/IV in G major (G7).

lessons.title: The secondary dominants of C
lessons.teaches: A major key has five secondary dominants, one for each major or minor diatonic chord except I.
facts: In C major the secondary dominants are A7 (V7/ii), B7 (V7/iii), C7 (V7/IV), D7 (V7/V) and E7 (V7/vi).
There is no V/vii°, because a diminished chord cannot act as a temporary tonic.
Each one contains at least one note outside the key, usually the leading tone of its target: C# in A7, F# in D7, G# in E7.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord boxes of A7 (x02020), B7 (x21202), C7 (x32310), D7 (xx0212) and E7 (020100), each over its target chord; audio of each resolving.

exercises.idea: Match in C: A7 / V7/ii, B7 / V7/iii, D7 / V7/V, E7 / V7/vi.
Which outside note does E7 add in C major? (G#)
C major has a secondary dominant for vii° (false).

lessons.title: Spotting and resolving them
lessons.teaches: A major or dominant chord where the key has a minor chord is usually a secondary dominant, and it usually resolves down a fifth.
facts: A major or dominant-7th chord on a degree where the key has a minor chord is often a secondary dominant: A7 in C, where the key's chord is Am.
Secondary dominants usually resolve down a fifth to their target: E7 to Am.
Outside a blues, I7 (C7 in C) usually heads to IV, so it is heard as V7/IV rather than as the tonic.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: an original eight-bar chart in G (| G | E7 | Am | D7 | G | B7 | Em | D7 |) with chord boxes (G 320003, E7 020100, Am x02210, D7 xx0212, B7 x21202, Em 022000), the secondary dominants circled and arrows to their targets; audio.

exercises.idea: In G major, B7 resolves to which chord? (Em)
Did the secondary dominant resolve to its target or not?
In D major, type the target chord of F#7 (Bm).

lessons.title: Chains of dominants
lessons.teaches: Dominants can chain, each resolving down a fifth to the next, travelling round the circle of fifths toward the tonic.
facts: Dominant chords can chain, each resolving down a fifth to the next dominant: E7 A7 D7 G7 C.
Such a chain travels anticlockwise round the circle of fifths toward the tonic.
The "ragtime progression" is III7-VI7-II7-V7-I: E7 A7 D7 G7 C in C major.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play E7 (020100), A7 (x02020), D7 (xx0212), G7 (320001), C (x32010). Figure: the circle of fifths with the chain drawn as arrows; audio.

exercises.idea: Order the chain ending on C: G7, E7, D7, A7 (E7, A7, D7, G7).
What dominant comes before E7 in a chain of fifths? (B7)
Play the ragtime progression in C.

lessons.title: Secondary leading-tone chords
lessons.teaches: A diminished chord a half step below a diatonic chord can lead to it, acting as a dominant without its root.
facts: A secondary leading-tone chord is the vii° or vii°7 of a chord other than the tonic: F#dim7 leading to G in C (vii°7/V).
It works like a secondary dominant without its root: F#dim7 (F# A C Eb) is D7b9 (D F# A C Eb) without the D.
Its root is a half step below the root of its target chord.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play C (x32010), F#dim7 (2x121x), G (320003). Figure: chord boxes with the F# to G bass step marked; audio.

exercises.idea: Which diminished seventh chord leads to Am in C? (G#dim7)
F#dim7 = F# A C _ (Eb).
Did a diminished chord lead to the next chord a half step up?

lessons.title: Hearing secondary dominants
lessons.teaches: The clue to a secondary dominant is a major chord where you expected a minor one, pulling strongly to the next chord.
facts: I-VI7-ii-V7 (C A7 Dm G7) uses a secondary dominant to make ii sound like a destination.
Hearing a major chord where the key would have a minor one is the clue to a secondary dominant.
Many secondary dominants are open shapes on guitar: A7, B7, D7 and E7.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Audio: I-vi-ii-V and I-VI7-ii-V7 in C, played with C (x32010), Am (x02210), A7 (x02020), Dm (xx0231) and G7 (320001), and the same in G. Figure: chord boxes revealed after each answer.

exercises.idea: I-vi-ii-V or I-VI7-ii-V7?
Play C A7 Dm G7.
Which chord was the secondary dominant: the 2nd, 3rd or 4th?

units.checkpoint: V/x notation and tonicization; the five secondary dominants of C and why vii° has none; the outside note each one adds; spotting and resolving them; chains of dominants around the circle and the ragtime progression; vii°7/x as a rootless dominant with b9; hearing I-VI7-ii-V7.

units.title: Modal harmony and borrowed chords
units.summary: Building chord progressions in a mode, and borrowing chords from the parallel minor and other modes.
units.whyItMatters: These are the colours behind rock's bVII, the bittersweet minor iv and the modal sound of much film and folk music.

lessons.title: Progressions in a mode
lessons.teaches: Modal harmony centres on the mode's own tonic chord, leans on its characteristic chord and avoids the V7-I that would pull to the parent major key.
facts: Modal progressions avoid a strong V7-I, which would pull the ear to the parent major key.
Each mode has a characteristic chord containing its characteristic note: Dorian IV, Mixolydian bVII, Lydian II, Phrygian bII, Aeolian bVI.
A two-chord vamp of the tonic and the characteristic chord establishes a mode clearly: Dm to G for D Dorian.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Vamp each pair: Dm (xx0231) to G (320003) for D Dorian, G to F (133211) for G Mixolydian, F (133211) to G for F Lydian, Em (022000) to F (133211) for E Phrygian, Am (x02210) to F for A Aeolian. Figure: chord boxes with the characteristic note circled in each second chord; audio.

exercises.idea: Match each mode to its characteristic chord: Dorian / IV, Mixolydian / bVII, Lydian / II, Phrygian / bII.
Which mode does this two-chord vamp suggest?
Which chord gives A Mixolydian its colour? (G)

lessons.title: Drones and chords in fourths
lessons.teaches: A drone on the tonic holds a mode in place, and chords stacked in fourths support modal music without pointing to a major or minor key.
facts: A drone or pedal on the tonic holds a mode in place while chords or melody move above it.
Open strings make modal drones easy: E Phrygian or E Dorian over open string 6, D Mixolydian over open string 4.
Quartal voicings stack fourths (D G C on strings 5, 4, 3 at fret 5, x555xx) and do not imply a major or minor chord.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Over a ringing open string 4 (D), move the quartal shape x555xx and its neighbours along D Dorian. Figure: tab of the moving fourths over the drone; audio.

exercises.idea: Place the quartal shape D G C on strings 5, 4, 3 at fret 5 (x555xx).
Do these chords suggest major, minor, or neither?
Over a drone on open string 6, which modes are easiest to explore? (E modes, such as E Phrygian or E Dorian)

lessons.title: Borrowing from the parallel minor
lessons.teaches: Modal interchange borrows a chord from a parallel key or mode with the same tonic, changing the colour without changing the key.
facts: Modal interchange (borrowing) takes a chord from a parallel key or mode, with the same tonic, and uses it in the home key.
In C major, chords borrowed from C minor include Fm (iv), Ab (bVI), Bb (bVII) and Eb (bIII).
Borrowed chords keep the same tonic: they change the colour, not the key.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play C (x32010), Fm (133111), C; then C, Ab (466544), Bb (x13331), C. Figure: chord boxes with the borrowed notes (Ab, Bb, Eb) highlighted; audio.

exercises.idea: Which chord is borrowed from C minor: F, Fm or Dm? (Fm)
In G major, type the borrowed bVII (F).
Was the IV chord major or minor?

lessons.title: The minor iv
lessons.teaches: The minor iv in a major key adds a bittersweet colour, because its flat 6th falls a half step to the tonic chord's 5th.
facts: The minor iv chord in a major key (Fm in C) adds a bittersweet colour, often just before I.
Its b6 (Ab in C) falls a half step to the 5th of the tonic chord (G).
IV-iv-I (F Fm C) is a common, gentle ending.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play F (133211), Fm (133111), C (x32010): only string 3 changes between F and Fm (A to Ab). Figure: chord boxes with the moving voice; audio.

exercises.idea: Play IV-iv-I in C: F, Fm, C.
In the F to Fm change, tap the note that moves (string 3, fret 2 to fret 1).
IV-I or IV-iv-I?

lessons.title: bVII and bVI
lessons.teaches: bVII and bVI, borrowed from the minor key, give rock and film music some of their most recognisable progressions.
facts: bVII (Bb in C), borrowed from minor or Mixolydian, gives rock the progression I-bVII-IV (C Bb F).
bVI-bVII-I (Ab Bb C in C) is a common rock and film-music cadence.
bIII (Eb in C) is another borrowing from the parallel minor.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play A (x02220), G (320003), D (xx0232) for I-bVII-IV in A; then F, G, A for bVI-bVII-I in A. Figure: chord boxes with numerals; audio.

exercises.idea: In D major, type bVI (Bb).
Did the cadence go V-I or bVI-bVII-I?
Play F, G, A (bVI-bVII-I in A).

lessons.title: The Neapolitan and the borrowed iiø7
lessons.teaches: Two more chromatic chords lead to V: the Neapolitan (a major chord on the flat 2nd, as in Phrygian) and the half-diminished ii borrowed from minor.
facts: The Neapolitan chord is a major chord on the flat 2nd degree (Db in C), usually in first inversion (Db/F), leading to V.
In C minor, the Neapolitan Db/F typically moves to G or G7 and then to Cm.
iiø7 (Dm7b5 in C), borrowed from C minor, makes a darker ii-V-I: Dm7b5 G7 C.
lessons.onTheGuitar: In A minor, play Am (x02210), Bb/D (xx0331, the Neapolitan in first inversion), E7 (020100), Am. Figure: chord boxes with the bass line marked; audio.

exercises.idea: Type the Neapolitan chord of E minor (F).
Which inversion is the Neapolitan usually in? (first)
Did the ii-V-I use Dm7 or Dm7b5?

units.checkpoint: Modal harmony: the tonic as the mode's first chord, avoiding V7-I, each mode's characteristic chord, vamps, drones and quartal voicings; modal interchange from the parallel minor (iv, bVI, bVII, bIII, iiø7); IV-iv-I and bVI-bVII-I; the Neapolitan chord.

units.title: Jazz harmony basics
units.summary: The major and minor ii-V-I, guide tones, shell, drop-2 and drop-3 voicings, turnarounds and comping.
units.whyItMatters: With ii-V-Is, guide tones and a handful of voicings you can play through most jazz standards.

lessons.title: The major ii-V-I
lessons.teaches: The major ii-V-I is iim7, V7, Imaj7, with roots falling in fifths.
facts: The major ii-V-I uses iim7, V7 and Imaj7: Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 in C.
Its roots move down in fifths (D G C), often called the strongest root motion in tonal harmony.
Many jazz standards are built from ii-V-I progressions in several keys.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play Am7 (x02010), D7 (xx0212), Gmaj7 (3x443x) for ii-V-I in G. Figure: chord boxes over a circle-of-fifths arrow; audio.

exercises.idea: ii-V-I in F: Gm7, _, Fmaj7 (C7).
Type the ii chord of a ii-V-I in Bb (Cm7).
Is this a ii-V-I?

lessons.title: The minor ii-V-i
lessons.teaches: The minor ii-V-i uses a half-diminished ii, a dominant V (often with b9) and a minor tonic.
facts: The minor ii-V-i uses iiø7, V7 and a minor tonic: Bm7b5 E7 Am (or Am6, or the minor-major seventh AmMaj7) in A minor.
A half-diminished chord (m7b5, ø7) is a diminished triad plus a minor 7th: Bm7b5 is B D F A.
The b9 of E7 (F) belongs to A harmonic minor, which is why V7b9 sounds natural in a minor key.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play Bm7b5 (x2323x), E7 (020100), Am6 (x02212). Figure: chord boxes with function labels; audio.

exercises.idea: Minor ii-V-i in D minor: Em7b5, _, Dm (A7).
Type the b9 of E7b9 (F).
Major ii-V-I or minor ii-V-i?

lessons.title: Guide tones
lessons.teaches: The 3rd and 7th of each chord are its guide tones, and through a ii-V-I each 7th falls a half step to the next chord's 3rd.
facts: Guide tones are the 3rd and 7th of each chord: they define its quality.
In ii-V-I the 7th of each chord falls a half step to the 3rd of the next: C (7th of Dm7) to B (3rd of G7), F (7th of G7) to E (3rd of Cmaj7).
The other guide tone stays put: F, the 3rd of Dm7, becomes the 7th of G7; B, the 3rd of G7, becomes the 7th of Cmaj7.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: two guide-tone lines on strings 3 and 2 through Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 (C-F, B-F, B-E: string 3 fret 5 and string 2 fret 6; string 3 fret 4 and string 2 fret 6; string 3 fret 4 and string 2 fret 5); audio.

exercises.idea: The 7th of G7 (F) falls to _, the 3rd of Cmaj7 (E).
Play the guide tones through Dm7 G7 Cmaj7 on strings 3 and 2.
Which notes are the guide tones of A7? (C# and G)

lessons.title: Shell voicings
lessons.teaches: A shell voicing plays only the root, 3rd and 7th, which is enough to sound any seventh chord.
facts: A shell voicing plays only the root, 3rd and 7th of a chord.
Shells with the root on string 6: Gmaj7 3x44xx, G7 3x34xx, Gm7 3x33xx.
Shells with the root on string 5: Cmaj7 x3x45x, C7 x3x35x, Cm7 x3x34x.
ii-V-I in C with shells moves by small steps: Dm7 x5x56x, G7 3x34xx, Cmaj7 x3x45x.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord boxes of the six shells, Gmaj7 3x44xx, G7 3x34xx, Gm7 3x33xx, Cmaj7 x3x45x, C7 x3x35x and Cm7 x3x34x, with dots labelled 1, 3 or b3, 7 or b7; then the shell ii-V-I; audio.

exercises.idea: Build an A7 shell with the root on string 6 (5x56xx).
Build an Fmaj7 shell with the root on string 5 (x-8-x-9-10-x).
Play the shell ii-V-I in C: x5x56x, 3x34xx, x3x45x.

lessons.title: Drop-2 voicings
lessons.teaches: A drop-2 voicing lowers the second-highest note of a close four-note chord by an octave, spreading it comfortably across four neighbouring strings.
facts: A drop-2 voicing takes a close-position four-note chord and drops its second-highest note an octave.
Drop-2 voicings sit on four neighbouring strings, such as strings 5 to 2 or 4 to 1.
Cmaj7 in root position as a drop-2 on strings 5 to 2 is x3545x (C G B E): it comes from the close voicing G B C E with the C dropped an octave.
Dropping the second-highest note of the close voicing C E G B gives G C E B instead: Cmaj7/G (3324xx), a drop-2 with the 5th in the bass.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: Cmaj7 in close position G B C E on a staff, the C dropped an octave to give C G B E, then the shape x3545x on strings 5 to 2; beside it, close C E G B with its G dropped to give G C E B, the shape Cmaj7/G (3324xx) on strings 6 to 3; audio of both.

exercises.idea: Place Cmaj7 drop 2 on strings 5 to 2 (x3545x).
Close Cmaj7 voiced G B C E, low to high: drop its second-highest note and order the result from low to high (C G B E).
Which note of a close voicing does drop 2 lower? (the second from the top)

lessons.title: Drop-3 voicings
lessons.teaches: A drop-3 voicing lowers the third-highest note of a close chord by an octave, leaving a gap above the bass, often on string 6 or 5.
facts: A drop-3 voicing drops the third-highest note of a close-position chord an octave.
Drop-3 voicings usually have the bass on string 6 or 5 and skip the next string.
Gmaj7 drop 3 with the root on string 6: 3x443x (G F# B D).
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord boxes of Gmaj7 (3x443x), G7 (3x343x) and Gm7 (3x333x) drop-3 shapes; audio.

exercises.idea: Place Gmaj7 drop 3 (3x443x).
In a drop-3 voicing, which string is usually skipped? (the one next to the bass)
Change Gmaj7 (3x443x) into G7 by lowering one note (3x343x).

lessons.title: Turnarounds
lessons.teaches: A turnaround is a short progression at the end of a section that leads back to I, and jazz uses a few standard ones.
facts: A turnaround is a short progression at the end of a section that leads back to I.
I-vi-ii-V (C Am7 Dm7 G7) is often played I-VI7-ii-V7 (C A7 Dm7 G7) to strengthen the pull.
iii-VI7-ii-V7 (Em7 A7 Dm7 G7) is another common turnaround, starting on a tonic substitute.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play Cmaj7 (x3545x), A7 (5x56xx), Dm7 (x5x56x), G7 (3x34xx). Figure: shells for the turnaround; audio.

exercises.idea: I-VI7-ii-V7 in F: Fmaj7, D7, Gm7, _ (C7).
I-vi-ii-V or iii-VI7-ii-V7?
Play the I-VI7-ii-V7 turnaround in C.

lessons.title: Comping
lessons.teaches: Comping is accompanying a soloist with chords, from steady four-to-the-bar to sparse, syncopated hits.
facts: Comping is accompanying a soloist with chords, placed rhythmically to support the music.
Swing-era rhythm guitarists often played short three-note chords on every beat, called four-to-the-bar comping.
Modern comping uses fewer, syncopated chord hits and leaves room for the soloist.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Over a ii-V-I loop in C with shells (Dm7 x5x56x, G7 3x34xx, Cmaj7 x3x45x): one bar of four short chords, then a bar with hits on the "&" of 1 and on beat 3 only. Figure: rhythm lines for both; audio.

exercises.idea: Tap four-to-the-bar comping for two bars, keeping each chord short.
Four-to-the-bar or syncopated comping?
Comping means playing as many chords as possible (false).

units.checkpoint: Major and minor ii-V-I chords in several keys; guide-tone motion (each 7th falls to the next 3rd); shell voicings with roots on strings 6 and 5 and a shell ii-V-I; drop-2 and drop-3 voicings and how they are made; the I-vi-ii-V, I-VI7-ii-V7 and iii-VI7-ii-V7 turnarounds; comping styles.

units.title: Altered dominants and substitutions
units.summary: Altered tensions, the 7#9 and 7alt chords, tritone substitution, the backdoor dominant and the diminished seventh as a dominant.
units.whyItMatters: These are the tensions and substitutions that make jazz, soul and blues-rock harmony sound sophisticated.

lessons.title: Altered tensions
lessons.teaches: A dominant chord can take altered tensions (b9, #9, #11, b13) that resolve by half step into the next chord.
facts: The altered tensions of a dominant 7th chord are b9, #9, #11 (the same pitch as b5) and b13 (the same pitch as #5).
Altered tensions usually resolve by half step into the next chord: the b9 of G7 (Ab) falls to G, the 5th of C.
G7b9 is G B D F Ab; G7#9 is G B D F A#.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: G7 (3x343x) and G7b9 (3231xx) resolving to Cmaj7, with the Ab-G voice marked; audio.

exercises.idea: Type the b13 of C7 (Ab).
Plain G7 or G7b9?
In G7 to C, where does the b9 (Ab) usually go? (down a half step to G)

lessons.title: The 7#9 chord
lessons.teaches: The 7#9 chord contains a major 3rd and a #9 that sounds like a minor 3rd an octave up, giving its gritty, bluesy clash.
facts: The 7#9 chord has a major 3rd and a #9 that sounds like a minor 3rd an octave higher, which gives it a gritty, bluesy sound.
A common E7#9 shape is x7678x: root E, 3rd G#, b7 D, and the #9 on string 2.
In E7#9 the #9 is spelled F##, even though it sounds like G.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: chord box of E7#9 (x7678x) with dots labelled 1, 3, b7, #9; moved down two frets it is D7#9 (x5456x); audio.

exercises.idea: Place E7#9 (x7678x).
Type the #9 of C7#9 (D#).
In E7#9 the #9 is correctly spelled G (false).

lessons.title: 7alt and the altered scale
lessons.teaches: A 7alt chord is a dominant with altered tensions chosen by the player, and the altered scale contains every one of them.
facts: A 7alt chord is a dominant 7th whose altered tensions (any of b9, #9, #11, b13) are chosen by the player.
The altered scale, the seventh mode of melodic minor, contains all of them: G altered is G Ab Bb Cb Db Eb F.
G altered has the same notes as Ab melodic minor.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: G altered in one position around fret 3, each note labelled with its job over G7: 1 (G), b9 (Ab), #9 (spelled Bb), 3 (spelled Cb), #11 (spelled Db), b13 (Eb), b7 (F); audio over G7alt resolving to C.

exercises.idea: Which melodic minor has the same notes as E altered? (F)
Over G7, Mixolydian or altered?
G altered: G Ab Bb _ Db Eb F (Cb).

lessons.title: Tritone substitution
lessons.teaches: A dominant 7th can be replaced by the dominant 7th a tritone away, because the two chords share the same tritone.
facts: A tritone substitute replaces a dominant 7th chord with the dominant 7th a tritone away: Db7 for G7, written subV7.
G7 (G B D F) and Db7 (Db F Ab Cb) share the same tritone, B and F, which Db7 spells Cb and F.
Dm7 Db7 Cmaj7 gives a chromatic bass line falling D, Db, C.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play Dm7 (x5x56x), Db7 (x4x46x), Cmaj7 (x3x45x): the bass slides down a fret at a time. Figure: the shells with the shared tritone circled in G7 and Db7; audio.

exercises.idea: Type the tritone substitute of D7 (Ab7).
ii-V-I or ii-subV-I?
Which two notes do G7 and Db7 share in sound? (B/Cb and F)

lessons.title: The backdoor dominant
lessons.teaches: bVII7 can resolve to I like a dominant, often after the minor iv: the backdoor progression.
facts: The backdoor dominant is bVII7 resolving to I: Bb7 to C in C major.
iv7-bVII7-I (Fm7 Bb7 C) is called the backdoor ii-V.
Bb7 contains D, F and Ab, three of the notes of G7b9, which is why it can lead home like a dominant.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play Fm7 (131111), Bb7 (x13131), Cmaj7 (x3545x). Figure: chord boxes with the shared notes highlighted; audio of ii-V-I and the backdoor version.

exercises.idea: In G major, type the backdoor dominant (F7).
Front door (V7-I) or backdoor (bVII7-I)?
Play Fm7, Bb7, Cmaj7.

lessons.title: The diminished seventh as a dominant
lessons.teaches: A diminished seventh chord on the leading tone is a dominant b9 chord without its root, so it can replace V7.
facts: Bdim7 (B D F Ab) is G7b9 (G B D F Ab) without the G.
So vii°7 can stand in for V7: Bdim7 to C works like G7b9 to C.
A dim7 chord a half step below any chord can lead into it, as a rootless dominant b9 of that chord.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play Bdim7 (x2313x), then C (x32010); then G7b9 (3231xx) to C. Figure: both chords with the shared four notes marked; audio.

exercises.idea: Bdim7 is which dominant chord without its root? (G7b9)
Type the dim7 chord that leads to D (C#dim7).
Did the dim7 resolve up a half step?

units.checkpoint: The altered tensions b9, #9, #11 and b13 and how they resolve; spelling G7b9, G7#9 (A#) and E7#9 (F##); the 7#9 shape; 7alt and the altered scale as the seventh mode of melodic minor; the tritone substitute and its shared tritone; the backdoor bVII7; vii°7 as a rootless V7b9.

units.title: Diminished, augmented and whole-tone sounds
units.summary: Chords and scales that divide the octave equally: diminished sevenths, diminished scales, augmented triads and the whole-tone scale.
units.whyItMatters: Symmetry makes these sounds easy to move around the neck, and they supply much of the drama in jazz, film and classical music.

lessons.title: The symmetry of the diminished seventh
lessons.teaches: A diminished seventh chord is all minor thirds, so it repeats every three frets and there are only three different ones.
facts: A diminished seventh chord is built entirely of minor thirds, so it divides the octave into four equal parts.
Moving a dim7 shape up three frets gives the same four notes in a new inversion.
There are only three different dim7 chords, on C, C# and D; every other dim7 has the same notes as one of these.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the shape x2313x (Bdim7) at frets 2, 5, 8 and 11, all labelled with the same four pitch names; audio.

exercises.idea: Move Bdim7 (x2313x) up three frets and play it (x5646x).
Which dim7 has the same notes as Bdim7: Ddim7 or Edim7? (Ddim7)
There are twelve different diminished seventh chords (false).

lessons.title: One diminished chord, four dominants
lessons.teaches: Because any note of a dim7 can be its root, one dim7 works as a rootless 7b9 chord for four different dominants, and as a passing chord.
facts: One dim7 is the rootless 7b9 of four dominants: the notes of Bdim7 work for G7b9, Bb7b9, Db7b9 and E7b9.
A passing diminished chord connects two chords a whole step apart: C, C#dim7, Dm7.
A common-tone diminished chord decorates a chord with the same root: C, Cdim7, C.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play C (x32010), C#dim7 (x4535x), Dm7 (xx0211). Figure: the rising bass C C# D marked; audio.

exercises.idea: Which dominants can Bdim7 stand in for? (G7b9, Bb7b9, Db7b9, E7b9)
Type the passing dim7 between G and Am (G#dim7).
Passing diminished chord or not?

lessons.title: The diminished scales
lessons.teaches: The two diminished scales alternate half and whole steps; half-whole fits dominant 7b9 chords and whole-half fits diminished sevenths.
facts: The half-whole diminished scale alternates half and whole steps from the root: C Db Eb E F# G A Bb.
It fits dominant 7b9 chords: C half-whole over C7b9.
The whole-half diminished scale (C D Eb F Gb Ab A B) fits diminished seventh chords.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: C half-whole diminished on strings 5 to 2 around fret 3 with the C7 chord tones highlighted; audio over C7b9.

exercises.idea: C half-whole: C Db Eb E F# _ A Bb (G).
Over G7b9: Mixolydian or half-whole diminished?
Which diminished scale fits Cdim7? (whole-half)

lessons.title: The augmented triad
lessons.teaches: An augmented triad is two major thirds, dividing the octave into three, so it repeats every four frets.
facts: An augmented triad is two major thirds and divides the octave into three equal parts.
Moving an augmented shape up four frets gives the same notes: Caug, Eaug and G#aug share the pitches C, E and G#.
There are only four different augmented triads.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: Caug on strings 4-3-2 (10-9-9) moved down four frets (6-5-5: G# C E, the same three pitches) and down four more (2-1-1: E G# C, the same pitches again); audio.

exercises.idea: Place the augmented triad on strings 4-3-2 at frets 6-5-5: the same three pitches as Caug at 10-9-9.
Eaug and Caug contain the same pitches (true).
Augmented or major triad?

lessons.title: The whole-tone scale
lessons.teaches: The whole-tone scale has six notes a whole step apart, there are only two of them, and it fits dominant 7#5 chords.
facts: The whole-tone scale has six notes, each a whole step apart: C D E F# G# Bb.
There are only two whole-tone scales: one starting on C and one on C# (or Db).
It fits dominant chords with a #5 (C7#5, also written C7+); having no half steps, it sounds dreamlike and unresolved.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: C whole tone along string 5 (frets 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15) and in one position across all six strings; audio over C7#5.

exercises.idea: C whole tone: C D E _ G# Bb (F#).
Whole-tone scale or major scale?
How many different whole-tone scales are there? (2)

lessons.title: Augmented chords in progressions
lessons.teaches: Augmented chords move: a rising 5th turns I into IV, and V+ pushes harder toward I.
facts: A rising line from the 5th, C Caug C6 C7 (G G# A Bb), is a common way to move from I to IV.
V+ (G+ = G B D#) strengthens the pull to I, because its D# rises to E.
Harmonic minor contains an augmented chord on bIII: Caug in A minor.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play C (x32010), Caug (x32110), C6 (x32210: the 5th has moved up to the 6th, so this shape can also be read as Am/C), C7 (x32310), F. Figure: string 3 rising G G# A Bb (frets 0, 1, 2, 3); audio.

exercises.idea: Play C, Caug, C6, C7, F with the rising voice on string 3.
Type the raised 5th of G+ (D#).
V-I or V+-I?

units.checkpoint: The dim7 chord as stacked minor thirds, its four-way symmetry and the three distinct dim7 chords; one dim7 as a rootless 7b9 for four dominants; passing and common-tone diminished chords; the half-whole and whole-half diminished scales and their chords; the augmented triad's three-way symmetry; the two whole-tone scales and 7#5; the augmented chord in a rising line and as V+.

units.title: Scales beyond the basics
units.summary: Chord-scale thinking, the modes of melodic and harmonic minor, bebop scales, exotic scales and pentatonic superimposition.
units.whyItMatters: These scales give you a precise colour for every chord, from Lydian dominant to Phrygian dominant to the altered scale.

lessons.title: A scale for every chord
lessons.teaches: Chord-scale thinking matches each chord with a scale containing its chord tones and suitable tensions, and marks the notes to avoid holding.
facts: Chord-scale thinking matches each chord with a scale that contains its chord tones and suitable tensions.
The usual scales for the diatonic seventh chords are their modes: Imaj7 Ionian, iim7 Dorian, V7 Mixolydian, viiø7 Locrian.
An avoid note is a scale note a half step above a chord tone that clashes if held: the 4 (F) over Cmaj7.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: C Ionian in one position with the Cmaj7 tones coloured and F marked as the avoid note; audio of F held over Cmaj7 versus F passing to E.

exercises.idea: Match in C: Dm7 / D Dorian, G7 / G Mixolydian, Bm7b5 / B Locrian.
Which note is the avoid note over Cmaj7 in C Ionian? (F)
Was the clashing note held or passed through?

lessons.title: The modes of melodic minor
lessons.teaches: Melodic minor's modes supply the standard jazz colours for 7#11, m7b5, 7alt and maj7#5 chords.
facts: Mode 4 of melodic minor, Lydian dominant (1 2 3 #4 5 6 b7), fits 7#11 chords; G Lydian dominant has the notes of D melodic minor.
Mode 6, Locrian natural 2 (1 2 b3 4 b5 b6 b7), fits m7b5 chords.
Mode 7 is the altered scale (fits 7alt); mode 3, Lydian augmented (1 2 3 #4 #5 6 7), fits maj7#5.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: D melodic minor in one position, relabelled in turn from G (Lydian dominant), B (Locrian natural 2) and C# (altered); audio of each over its chord.

exercises.idea: Type the notes of G Lydian dominant (G A B C# D E F).
Match: 7#11 / Lydian dominant, m7b5 / Locrian natural 2, 7alt / altered, maj7#5 / Lydian augmented.
Over G7: Mixolydian or Lydian dominant?

lessons.title: Phrygian dominant
lessons.teaches: Phrygian dominant, mode 5 of harmonic minor, is the sound of V7b9 in a minor key and of much flamenco and metal guitar.
facts: Phrygian dominant (1 b2 3 4 5 b6 b7) is mode 5 of harmonic minor.
E Phrygian dominant is E F G# A B C D: the notes of A harmonic minor centred on E.
It is the sound of V7b9 in a minor key, and is central to flamenco and much metal guitar.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play E Phrygian dominant in open position over an E chord (022100); figure: open-position pattern with G# and F highlighted; audio of Am G F E with the scale over E.

exercises.idea: Type the notes of B Phrygian dominant (B C D# E F# G A).
E Phrygian or E Phrygian dominant?
Phrygian dominant is a mode of which scale? (harmonic minor)

lessons.title: Bebop scales
lessons.teaches: Bebop scales add one chromatic passing note so that eighth-note runs keep chord tones on the beats.
facts: Bebop scales add one chromatic passing note to a seven-note scale, so that eighth-note runs starting on a chord tone on the beat keep chord tones on the beats.
The bebop dominant scale is Mixolydian plus the major 7th: G A B C D E F F#.
The bebop major scale is the major scale plus #5: C D E F G G# A B.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: G bebop dominant descending in eighth notes from G on string 1 fret 3, with the beats marked: G, F, D and B fall on beats 1 to 4 and the G an octave lower lands on the next beat 1; audio over G7.

exercises.idea: G bebop dominant: G A B C D E F _ (F#).
Play G bebop dominant descending from G in eighth notes over G7.
Which note does bebop major add to C major? (G#)

lessons.title: Exotic scales
lessons.teaches: A few scales from outside the major-minor system give instantly recognisable colours on guitar.
facts: Hungarian minor is 1 2 b3 #4 5 b6 7: harmonic minor with a raised 4th (A B C D# E F G# in A).
Double harmonic is 1 b2 3 4 5 b6 7, with two augmented seconds (b2 to 3 and b6 to 7).
Hirajoshi (1 2 b3 5 b6) and In (1 b2 4 5 b6) are Japanese pentatonic scales.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: A Hungarian minor and A hirajoshi in fifth position with their characteristic notes highlighted; audio of each over an A drone.

exercises.idea: Type the notes of E double harmonic (E F G# A B C D#).
Hungarian minor or harmonic minor?
How many notes does hirajoshi have? (5)

lessons.title: Pentatonics on other roots
lessons.teaches: Playing a pentatonic scale on a different root than the chord adds chosen colour tones while keeping familiar shapes.
facts: Over Am7, B minor pentatonic (B D E F# A) gives the 9, 11, 5, 6 and root: a Dorian colour.
Over Cmaj7, D major pentatonic (D E F# A B) gives the 9, 3, #11, 13 and 7: a Lydian colour.
Over G7alt, Bb minor pentatonic (Bb Db Eb F Ab) gives the #9, b5, b13, b7 and b9.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: box 1 of B minor pentatonic at fret 7 drawn over an Am7 voicing, each note labelled with its degree against A; audio over Am7.

exercises.idea: Over Cmaj7, which pentatonic gives a Lydian colour: D major or G major pentatonic? (D major)
Over Am7, which degree is F# in B minor pentatonic? (6)
Over G7alt: G minor pentatonic or Bb minor pentatonic?

units.checkpoint: Chord-scale matching and avoid notes; melodic minor and its modes (Lydian dominant for 7#11, Locrian natural 2 for m7b5, altered for 7alt, Lydian augmented for maj7#5); Phrygian dominant for V7b9 in minor; the bebop dominant and bebop major scales and why the passing note helps; Hungarian minor, double harmonic and Japanese pentatonic scales; pentatonic superimposition.

units.title: Voice leading
units.summary: How the notes of one chord move to the next: common tones, motion types, parallel fifths, line clichés, non-chord tones and smooth seventh chords.
units.whyItMatters: Good voice leading makes simple progressions sound polished and makes chord changes easier for your hand.

lessons.title: What voice leading is
lessons.teaches: Voice leading is how each note of a chord moves to the next chord, and smooth voice leading keeps common tones and moves by small steps.
facts: Voice leading is how the individual notes (voices) of one chord move to the notes of the next.
Smooth voice leading keeps common tones and moves the other voices by the smallest steps.
C to Am keeps C and E and moves only G up to A.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: C (x32010) to Am (x02210): strings 4, 2 and 1 keep E, C and E; string 3 moves G to A; the bass moves C to A; audio.

exercises.idea: Going from C to Am, which notes stay? (C and E)
Smooth or jumpy voice leading?
From C (x32010) to Am (x02210), tap the two new notes of Am, both A, between frets 0 and 3 (open string 5, string 3 fret 2).

lessons.title: Choosing inversions for smooth changes
lessons.teaches: Choosing inversions that keep common tones on the same strings keeps your hand in one place and the voices moving by small steps.
facts: Choosing inversions that keep common tones on the same strings makes chord changes smoother.
On strings 3-2-1, G (4-3-3), C (5-5-3) and D (2-3-2) keep the hand within frets 2 to 5.
Between G (4-3-3) and C (5-5-3), string 1 keeps G while B and D step up to C and E.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the three triads on strings 3-2-1 within frets 2 to 5 with arrows showing each voice's move; audio of I-IV-V-I.

exercises.idea: From G (4-3-3) to C (5-5-3), which string keeps its note? (string 1)
Place D in second inversion on strings 3-2-1 (frets 2, 3, 2).

lessons.title: Parallel, similar, contrary, oblique
lessons.teaches: Two voices can move in parallel, similar, contrary or oblique motion, and contrary motion makes parts most independent.
facts: Parallel motion: voices move the same direction by the same interval. Similar: same direction, different intervals.
Contrary motion: voices move in opposite directions. Oblique motion: one voice holds while the other moves.
Holding an open string while a fretted line moves is oblique motion on guitar.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: four two-voice tab examples on strings 1 and 3, one per motion type; audio.

exercises.idea: Match each example to its motion: parallel, similar, contrary, oblique.
Do the two voices move in contrary or parallel motion?
An open string rings while a melody moves above it. Which motion? (oblique)

lessons.title: Parallel fifths and the rule of style
lessons.teaches: Classical part writing avoids parallel fifths and octaves, but that is a rule of style: rock riffs are built on them, and parallel thirds and sixths are welcome everywhere.
facts: In classical part writing, two voices moving in parallel perfect fifths or octaves are avoided, because they weaken the independence of the parts.
Power-chord riffs are made entirely of parallel fifths; the rule belongs to a style, not to all music.
Parallel thirds and sixths are welcome in almost every style and are the sound of harmonised guitar lines.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: a four-chord progression voiced with parallel fifths and then corrected by contrary motion, plus a line in parallel sixths on strings 3 and 1; audio.

exercises.idea: Parallel fifths or parallel thirds?
Parallel fifths are wrong in every style of music (false).
Play G major in sixths on strings 3 and 1 (frets 0-0, 2-2, 4-3, 5-5, 7-7, 9-8, 11-10, 12-12).

lessons.title: Line clichés
lessons.teaches: A line cliché holds a chord while one voice moves chromatically, turning one chord into a moving progression.
facts: A line cliché keeps a chord while one voice, often an inner voice or the bass, moves chromatically: Am, AmMaj7, Am7, Am6 (A G# G F#).
On guitar, hold Am as xx7555 and move only string 4 down a fret at a time (frets 6, 5, 4): AmMaj7/G#, Am7/G, Am6/F#.
The same idea on a major chord moves the 5th up: C, Caug, C6, C7.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the four shapes on strings 4 to 1 with the moving voice on string 4 (frets 7, 6, 5, 4); audio.

exercises.idea: Play Am, AmMaj7, Am7, Am6 moving only string 4.
Line cliché voice: A, G#, G, _ (F#).
Is the moving voice rising or falling?

lessons.title: Notes outside the chord
lessons.teaches: Melody notes outside the chord are non-chord tones, named by how they move: passing tones, neighbour tones, suspensions and appoggiaturas.
facts: A passing tone moves by step between two different chord tones: over C, the D in C D E.
A neighbour tone steps away from a chord tone and back to it: over C, the F in E F E.
A suspension holds a note over from the previous chord, where it clashes, then resolves down by step: G held from a G chord into D, then falling to F#, is a 4-3 suspension.
An appoggiatura leaps to a non-chord tone on a strong beat and then resolves by step.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Over C (x32010), play string 2 frets 1, 3, 5 (C D E, the D passing) and string 1 frets 0, 1, 0 (E F E, the F a neighbour); then play G (320003), Dsus4 (xx0233) and D (xx0232), keeping string 1 at fret 3 (G) until it falls to F# at fret 2. Figure: tab with each non-chord tone labelled; audio.

exercises.idea: Match each non-chord tone to its motion: passing tone / steps between two chord tones, neighbour tone / steps away and back, suspension / held over then falls by step, appoggiatura / leaps in then steps.
Over a C chord the melody plays E F E. What is the F? (a neighbour tone)
Play G (320003), Dsus4 (xx0233), D (xx0232), holding string 1 at fret 3 until the last chord.
Did the held note resolve down by step?

lessons.title: A voice-led ii-V-I
lessons.teaches: With four-note voicings, each voice of a ii-V-I can move by a step or stay, so the hand barely moves.
facts: With four-note voicings, each voice of a ii-V-I can stay or move by a step.
Dm7 x5756x, G7 x5546x (with D in the bass), Cmaj7 x3545x: no voice moves more than a whole step.
Guide tones move by half step: C to B and F to E.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the three drop-2 voicings on strings 5 to 2, each voice drawn as a line; audio slow, then in time.

exercises.idea: Play Dm7 x5756x, G7 x5546x, Cmaj7 x3545x.
From Dm7 (x5756x) to G7 (x5546x), which voices stay? (D on string 5 and F on string 2)
Voice-led or jumpy ii-V-I?

units.checkpoint: Keeping common tones and moving by the smallest steps; choosing guitar inversions that keep common tones; parallel, similar, contrary and oblique motion; the classical rule against parallel fifths and octaves and where it does not apply; parallel thirds and sixths; line clichés; passing tones, neighbour tones, suspensions and appoggiaturas; a voice-led ii-V-I with four-note voicings.

units.title: Modulation and chromatic chords
units.summary: Changing key: tonicization versus modulation, related keys, pivot chords, direct key changes, chromatic mediants and augmented sixth chords.
units.whyItMatters: Key changes give songs and pieces their sense of journey, and recognising them stops a chart full of strange chords from being confusing.

lessons.title: Visiting or moving
lessons.teaches: Modulation is a lasting change of key confirmed by a cadence; tonicization is only a brief visit.
facts: Modulation is a change of key that lasts: a new tonic is established.
Tonicization is a brief visit, such as a secondary dominant and its target, after which the music returns to the home key.
A modulation is confirmed by a cadence in the new key.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play two original eight-bar passages in C with open chords (C x32010, F xx3211, Am x02210, D7 xx0212, G 320003): one with a single D7-G visit that returns to C, one that moves to G and cadences there (D7 G repeated, ending on G). Figure: both charts with the new key marked; audio.

exercises.idea: Did the passage visit G briefly or move to G for good?
What confirms a modulation? (a cadence in the new key)
Every secondary dominant is a modulation (false).

lessons.title: Closely related keys
lessons.teaches: Closely related keys differ by at most one sharp or flat, and they are the usual destinations of a modulation.
facts: Closely related keys differ by at most one sharp or flat: for C major they are G, F, A minor, E minor and D minor.
The most common modulation from a major key is to its dominant key: C to G.
Minor keys most often modulate to their relative major: A minor to C.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the circle of fifths with C, its neighbours G and F, and their relative minors Am, Em and Dm highlighted; on the neck, each tonic on strings 6 and 5: C at string 5 fret 3, G at string 6 fret 3, F at string 6 fret 1, A open string 5, E open string 6, D at string 5 fret 5.

exercises.idea: Which is closely related to G major: D major or Eb major? (D major)
Type the dominant key of F major (C major).
Match each key to its usual modulation: C major / G major, A minor / C major.

lessons.title: Pivot chords
lessons.teaches: A pivot chord belongs to both the old key and the new one, and it links them smoothly.
facts: A pivot chord belongs to both the old key and the new key and links them.
From C to G, Am is vi in C and ii in G, so C Am D7 G moves smoothly into G.
After the pivot, the new key's V and a cadence confirm the change.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play C (x32010), Am (x02210), D7 (xx0212), G (320003), holding the G as the new home. Figure: the chart with two rows of numerals, one in C and one in G, overlapping at Am; audio.

exercises.idea: From C to G, which chord can pivot: Am or Ab? (Am)
Em is iii in C and _ in G (vi).
Smooth pivot modulation or abrupt key change?

lessons.title: Direct and common-tone modulation
lessons.teaches: A direct modulation jumps to the new key without a pivot, and a common-tone modulation holds one shared note across the change.
facts: A direct (abrupt) modulation jumps to the new key without a pivot, often at the start of a new section.
Moving up a half step or whole step for a final chorus is a common pop key change.
A common-tone modulation holds one note shared by both keys while the harmony changes beneath it.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play an original four-bar chorus in G (G 320003, D xx0232, Em 022000, C x32010), then the same chorus up a whole step in A (A x02220, E 022100, F#m 244222, D xx0232). Figure: both charts; audio.

exercises.idea: Did the final chorus move up a half step or a whole step?
A chorus in E moves up a half step. Type the new key (F major).
A direct modulation needs a pivot chord (false).

lessons.title: Chromatic mediants
lessons.teaches: Chromatic mediants are chords with roots a third apart that share just one note, giving a striking, cinematic change.
facts: Chromatic mediants are chords of the same quality with roots a major or minor third apart that share only one note.
C to E shares only E; C to Ab shares only C.
They are common in film music and Romantic-era harmony.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Play C (x32010) to E (022100) and C to Ab (466544). Figure: chord boxes with the single shared note circled; audio.

exercises.idea: Which pair is a chromatic mediant: C to E, or C to F? (C to E)
Type the one note shared by C and Ab (C).
Chromatic mediant or ordinary diatonic change?

lessons.title: Augmented sixth chords
lessons.teaches: Augmented sixth chords put the flat 6th and the sharp 4th of the key a sixth apart, and these two notes spread outward to the 5th.
facts: Augmented sixth chords contain an augmented sixth between b6 and #4 of the key, which spread outward to an octave on the 5th: in C, Ab and F# move to G and G.
In C, the Italian sixth is Ab C F#, the French sixth Ab C D F#, and the German sixth Ab C Eb F#.
The German sixth sounds like an Ab7 chord with F# written instead of Gb; Ab7 is also the tritone substitute of D7, the V of V.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the three sixths in C as close voicings on strings 4 to 1 resolving to G (or C/G then G); staff showing Ab and F# moving out to G; audio.

exercises.idea: German sixth in C: Ab C Eb _ (F#).
Where does an augmented sixth chord usually resolve? (to V, or to I in second inversion then V)
Did the chord resolve outward to the dominant?

units.checkpoint: Tonicization versus modulation; closely related keys; modulating to the dominant and to the relative major; pivot chords; direct and common-tone modulation and the final-chorus key change; chromatic mediants; Italian, French and German sixth chords and how they resolve.

units.title: Improvising: playing the changes
units.summary: Horizontal and vertical playing, guide-tone lines, approach notes, enclosures, arpeggio substitution and outside playing.
units.whyItMatters: These are the tools for soloing over progressions that leave the key, from jazz standards to sophisticated pop.

lessons.title: One scale or every chord
lessons.teaches: Playing horizontally uses one scale for a whole passage; playing vertically follows each chord; good improvisers mix both.
facts: Playing horizontally means using one scale over a whole passage in one key; playing vertically means following each chord with its own tones or scale.
When every chord stays in one key, one scale can work; when chords leave the key, vertical playing is needed.
Most improvisers mix the two approaches.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Over C Am F G, play C major pentatonic with its root on string 6 fret 8 (frets 7 to 10) throughout; then over C A7 Dm G7, play chord tones of each chord in the same position (A7 adds C#, at string 6 fret 9). Figure: both progressions with the scale or arpeggios shown per bar; audio.

exercises.idea: Over C A7 Dm G7, which chord needs a note outside C major? (A7, with C#)
Did the solo follow each chord or stay on one scale?
Over A7, play an A7 arpeggio, then resolve to F on Dm.

lessons.title: Guide-tone lines
lessons.teaches: A guide-tone line is a slow melody of 3rds and 7ths that moves by step through the changes, and embellishing it gives a solo that follows the harmony.
facts: A guide-tone line is a simple melody made of the 3rds and 7ths of the chords, moving by step or staying.
Through Dm7 G7 Cmaj7, the line F, F, E (3rd of Dm7, 7th of G7, 3rd of Cmaj7) is a guide-tone line.
Solo by keeping the guide tones on the downbeats and decorating between them.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the guide-tone line F F E on string 2 (fret 6, 6, 5) under the chords, then the same line decorated with eighth notes in fifth position; audio.

exercises.idea: Guide-tone line through Dm7 G7 Cmaj7: C, B, _ (B).
Play the line F F E on string 2 over Dm7 G7 Cmaj7, one note per bar.
Does the solo land on guide tones at the changes?

lessons.title: Approach notes
lessons.teaches: An approach note leads into a target note by step, from the scale step above or a half step below.
facts: An approach note leads into a target note by step: from the scale note above or from a half step below.
A chromatic approach from a half step below works into almost any chord tone.
Placing the approach note on the off-beat lets the target land on the beat.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: targets E (3rd of C) on string 2 fret 5 approached from D# (fret 4) and from F (fret 6), with the target on the beat; audio over C.

exercises.idea: Type the half-step-below approach note to A (G#).
Over C, approach E from D# on the "&" of 4 and land on beat 1.
Did the line approach the target from above or below?

lessons.title: Enclosures
lessons.teaches: An enclosure surrounds a target note with notes above and below before landing on it, usually on a strong beat.
facts: An enclosure surrounds a target note with notes above and below it before landing on it.
A common enclosure plays the scale note above, then the half step below, then the target: F, D#, E targeting E.
Enclosures timed so the target lands on a strong beat are a hallmark of bebop.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab of F (string 2 fret 6), D# (fret 4), E (fret 5) arriving on beat 1 of a Cmaj7 bar; audio.

exercises.idea: Order an enclosure of C: B, D, C (D, B, C).
Play an enclosure of the 3rd of G7 (B) landing on beat 1: C, A#, B.
Was the target enclosed or approached from one side?

lessons.title: Arpeggios a third up
lessons.teaches: Playing the seventh arpeggio built on a chord's 3rd adds the 9th while keeping the 3rd, 5th and 7th.
facts: Over Cmaj7, an Em7 arpeggio (E G B D) gives the 3, 5, 7 and 9.
Over Dm7, an Fmaj7 arpeggio (F A C E) gives the b3, 5, b7 and 9.
Over G7, a Bm7b5 arpeggio (B D F A) gives the 3, 5, b7 and 9: a G9 sound without the root.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: an Em7 arpeggio from E on string 5 fret 7 (string 5 fret 7, string 4 frets 5 and 9, string 3 frets 7 and 9, string 2 fret 8, string 1 frets 7 and 10) drawn over Cmaj7 (x3545x), labelled 3 5 7 9; audio.

exercises.idea: Over Am7, which arpeggio starts on its 3rd? (Cmaj7)
Bm7b5 over G7 adds which extension? (the 9th)
Over Cmaj7: Cmaj7 arpeggio or Em7 arpeggio?

lessons.title: Going outside and coming back
lessons.teaches: Outside playing leaves the key on purpose for a moment and works when the phrase is clear and resolves back inside.
facts: Side-slipping moves a phrase a half step away from the key and back, creating tension that resolves.
Outside playing works when the outside phrase is clear and resolves convincingly back inside.
Playing Db7 ideas over G7 (tritone superimposition) is a standard outside sound.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Over a Dm7 vamp, play an original phrase in D minor pentatonic at fret 10, the same phrase a fret higher (Eb minor pentatonic), then back. Figure: tab of the three phrases; audio.

exercises.idea: Did the phrase slip outside and come back?
Over Dm7, play a phrase, slide it up a fret, then return it to the original fret.
Outside phrases work best when they never resolve (false).

units.checkpoint: Horizontal versus vertical playing; guide-tone lines through a ii-V-I; approach notes from a scale step above and a half step below; enclosures landing on strong beats; arpeggio substitution a third above the root; side-slipping and tritone superimposition.

units.title: Song form, arranging and writing
units.summary: Song sections and forms, phrases and periods, the guitar's roles in a band, chord melody, bass lines and writing your own progressions.
units.whyItMatters: Form and arranging turn chords you know into finished songs and parts that fit with other musicians.

lessons.title: Verse, chorus, bridge
lessons.teaches: Songs are built from sections with different jobs: the verse tells the story, the chorus repeats the main idea and the bridge brings contrast.
facts: A verse tells the story with changing lyrics over mostly the same music; a chorus repeats the main idea, usually with the same lyrics each time.
A bridge brings contrast, often with new chords, before a return to the chorus.
A pre-chorus builds from the verse into the chorus; an intro and an outro open and close the song.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: a song map of an original song (Intro, Verse, Pre-chorus, Chorus, Verse, Pre-chorus, Chorus, Bridge, Chorus, Outro) with the chords of each section in G as open shapes (G 320003, C x32010, D xx0232, Em 022000); audio of each section.

exercises.idea: Match each section to its job: verse / story, chorus / main idea repeated, bridge / contrast, intro / opening.
Is this section a verse or a chorus?
Put a typical verse-chorus song in order: chorus, verse, bridge, chorus (verse, chorus, bridge, chorus).

lessons.title: Forms by letter
lessons.teaches: Forms are described with letters for sections, from the 32-bar AABA song to classical binary, ternary and rondo forms.
facts: AABA, the 32-bar song form, has three 8-bar A sections and an 8-bar contrasting bridge (B).
Verse-chorus form alternates verses and choruses, often with a bridge near the end.
Classical forms include binary (AB), ternary (ABA) and rondo (ABACA).
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: letter diagrams of AABA, verse-chorus, binary, ternary and rondo, each letter played as an original four-bar strum in G on open chords (A: G 320003 and C x32010; B: Em 022000 and D xx0232); the 12-bar blues shown as one repeating A.

exercises.idea: How many bars does an AABA song form have? (32)
Match: AB / binary, ABA / ternary, ABACA / rondo.
Hear four sections: AABA or ABAB?

lessons.title: Phrases and periods
lessons.teaches: Music is built from phrases, often of 2, 4 or 8 bars, and two phrases ending in a half and then an authentic cadence make a period.
facts: Phrases are commonly 2, 4 or 8 bars long, and many song sections are 8 or 16 bars.
A period is two phrases: the first ends with a half cadence (the antecedent), the second with an authentic cadence (the consequent).
Listeners feel groups of four bars like large beats, which is why a 3-bar or 5-bar phrase sounds surprising.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: an original eight-bar period in G on the staff and in tab, the melody on strings 1 to 3 in first position over G (320003), C (x32010), D (xx0232) and D7 (xx0212), with the half cadence on D at bar 4 and the authentic cadence D7-G at bars 7-8; audio.

exercises.idea: Does this phrase end with a half cadence or an authentic cadence?
In a period, which phrase ends on V? (the first, the antecedent)
All phrases are exactly four bars long (false).

lessons.title: The guitar's jobs in a band
lessons.teaches: In a band the guitar plays rhythm, lead, riffs or fills, and two guitars sound fullest in different registers or voicings.
facts: In a band the guitar can play rhythm (chords), lead (melody and solos), riffs, or fills between vocal lines.
Two guitars sound fuller in different registers or voicings: one open chords, the other high triads or a capo.
With a bass player present, low root-heavy voicings can muddy the sound; higher voicings leave room for the bass.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the same G-D-Em-C progression as open chords for guitar 1 and as triads on strings 3-2-1 (or D shapes with capo 5) for guitar 2; audio of both together.

exercises.idea: Guitar 1 strums open chords. What should guitar 2 try? (higher triads or a capo position)
Are the two guitars in the same register or different registers?
Play G, D, Em, C as triads on strings 3-2-1.

lessons.title: Chord melody
lessons.teaches: A chord-melody arrangement puts the melody on top of the chords, so one guitar plays both.
facts: A chord-melody arrangement plays the melody as the top note of chords, so one guitar plays tune and harmony together.
Put the melody on string 1 or 2 and build a chord shape under each strong-beat melody note.
Between chords, single melody notes or small double stops keep the tune moving.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the first phrase of "Ode to Joy" (public domain) in C with the melody on strings 1 and 2 and a C or G chord shape under each beat 1; tab and audio.

exercises.idea: Play the chord-melody phrase, letting the melody note ring above each chord.
