The melody note is E over a C chord. Which C shape keeps E on top? (a shape with E on string 1, such as x32010)
Is the melody on top of the chords or hidden inside them?

lessons.title: Writing a bass line
lessons.teaches: A bass line plays chord roots on strong beats and connects them with 5ths, octaves and approach notes.
facts: A basic bass line plays the chord root on beat 1 and fills with 5ths, octaves and approach notes.
A walking bass line plays a note on every beat, moving mostly by step and landing on a chord tone at each change.
Approaching the next root by a half step on the last beat of the bar makes a change feel inevitable.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: tab of an original root-fifth bass line under G C D G on strings 6 to 4, then a walking version with half-step approaches; audio.

exercises.idea: Play a root-fifth bass line under G and C on strings 6 and 5.
Type a half-step approach note from below into C (B).
Root-fifth bass line or walking bass line?

lessons.title: Writing your own progression
lessons.teaches: Write a progression by choosing functions (home, away, tension, home), then colour it with borrowed or secondary chords.
facts: A progression can be planned by function: start at home, move away with subdominant chords, build tension with a dominant, and return.
Swapping one chord of a familiar progression for a borrowed or secondary chord gives it a fresh sound.
When adding a melody, put its long notes on chord tones and let passing notes fill between them.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: a worked example in G with open shapes: tonic-subdominant-dominant-tonic as G (320003), C (x32010), D (xx0232), G; then G Cm (x35543) D7 (xx0212) G for a borrowed iv, and G E7 (020100) Am (x02210) D7 G for a secondary dominant; audio of each.

exercises.idea: Order the functions of a basic progression: dominant, tonic, subdominant, tonic (tonic, subdominant, dominant, tonic).
Which chord would add a borrowed colour to G C D G: Cm or Em? (Cm)
Play G E7 Am D7 G.

units.title: Reading music: positions up the neck
units.summary: Positions and how they are marked, fifth position, choosing where to play, ledger lines above the staff and a sight-reading routine.
units.whyItMatters: Reading beyond first position opens up classical études, jazz heads and any melody written for another instrument.

lessons.title: Positions and how they are marked
lessons.teaches: A position is named after the fret under the first finger, and the music can mark both the position and the string.
facts: A position is named after the fret under the first finger: in fifth position the fingers cover frets 5 to 8.
Most notes can be played in several positions; the fingering or the markings show which one is meant.
Position is often marked with a roman numeral (V for fifth position); a circled number marks the string, so a circled 3 means play on string 3.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the written E in the top space (sounding E4) shown three ways: open string 1 (position I), string 2 fret 5 (position V, circled 2) and string 3 fret 9 (position IX, circled 3).

exercises.idea: Play written E (top space) on string 2 in fifth position (fret 5).
What does a circled 4 above a note mean? (play it on string 4)
In seventh position, which fret is under the first finger? (7)

lessons.title: Fifth position
lessons.teaches: In fifth position the natural notes lie under the four fingers at frets 5 to 8, with a stretch to fret 4 for B on string 3.
facts: Fifth-position naturals: string 6 A B C (frets 5, 7, 8); string 5 D E F (5, 7, 8); string 4 G A (5, 7); string 3 B C D (4, 5, 7); string 2 E F G (5, 6, 8); string 1 A B C (5, 7, 8).
The B on string 3 is reached by stretching the first finger back to fret 4.
The highest note in fifth position, string 1 fret 8, sounds C5 and is written two ledger lines above the staff.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard frets 4 to 8 with the fifth-position naturals and, above it, the staff from written A3 to C6 with each note joined to its fret; audio.

exercises.idea: In fifth position, tap every G (string 4 fret 5, string 2 fret 8).
Name the written note in the second space (A); in fifth position it is played at string 4 fret 7.
Read and play an original eight-bar melody in A minor in fifth position.

lessons.title: Choosing a position
lessons.teaches: Choose the position that keeps most of a passage under the hand, and shift where the move is easiest to hide.
facts: Choose the position that keeps most notes of a passage under the hand with the fewest shifts.
G major lies well in second position (frets 2 to 5); A minor lies well in fifth position and A major in fourth position (frets 4 to 7).
Shift during an open string, a repeated note or a rest, where the move is easiest to hide.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: an original eight-bar melody in G marked once with a bad fingering (three shifts) and once in second position (no shifts); audio.

exercises.idea: A melody in A minor spans A3 to C5. Which position suits it? (fifth position)
Was the shift smooth (during a rest) or audible?
The best position is always the lowest one (false).

lessons.title: Ledger lines above the staff and 8va
lessons.teaches: High notes use ledger lines above the staff, and 8va tells you to play an octave higher than written.
facts: The written A on the first ledger line above the staff sounds A4: string 1 fret 5.
The written C on the second ledger line above sounds C5: string 1 fret 8.
8va over a passage means play it an octave higher than written; loco means return to normal.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: staff from written G5 to E6 above string 1 frets 3 to 12, and a passage marked 8va with the frets it moves to; audio.

exercises.idea: Name the note on the first ledger line above the staff (A).
Tap where the written C on the second ledger line above is played (string 1, fret 8).
What does 8va mean? (play an octave higher than written)

lessons.title: A sight-reading routine
lessons.teaches: Before you play, scan the key, time, range and positions; then play slowly without stopping, reading ahead.
facts: Before playing, check the key signature, the time signature, the highest and lowest notes and any position changes.
Keep a slow, steady tempo: a wrong note is better than stopping.
Read ahead: look at the next beat or bar while you play the current one.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: an original sixteen-bar piece with a checklist panel (key, time, range, positions) to tick before the audio count-in starts.

exercises.idea: Order the checklist: play slowly without stopping, check the key signature, check the time signature, find the range (key, time, range, play).
Sight-read an original eight-bar melody at 60 BPM without stopping.
When sight-reading you should stop and fix every wrong note (false).

units.title: Tuning, harmonics and the physics of the string
units.summary: Frequency and concert pitch, what sets a string's pitch, the harmonic series, natural harmonics, fret spacing, equal temperament and alternate tunings.
units.whyItMatters: Knowing the physics explains harmonics, intonation and why a guitar can never be perfectly in tune in every key, and it lets you set up and retune your instrument with confidence.

lessons.title: Frequency and concert pitch
lessons.teaches: Concert pitch fixes A4 at 440 Hz, and every octave doubles the frequency.
facts: Concert pitch sets A4 at 440 Hz.
Each octave doubles the frequency: A2 (open string 5) is 110 Hz, A3 220 Hz and A4 440 Hz.
The open strings sound at about 82.4, 110, 146.8, 196, 246.9 and 329.6 Hz, from string 6 to string 1.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: the six open strings with their frequencies, and string 1 fret 5 (A4) labelled 440 Hz; tuner showing A4 = 440.

exercises.idea: What frequency is A3? (220 Hz)
Match each string to its frequency: 5 / 110 Hz, 3 / 196 Hz, 1 / 329.6 Hz.
Play A4 (string 1 fret 5), the note an orchestra tunes to.

lessons.title: Length, tension and mass
lessons.teaches: A string sounds higher when it is shorter, tighter or lighter.
facts: A string's pitch rises when it is shorter, tighter or lighter.
Frequency is inversely proportional to vibrating length: halving the length raises the pitch an octave.
Frequency is proportional to the square root of tension: raising a string an octave by tension alone would take four times the tension.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: three panels: fretting at fret 12 (half length), turning a peg (more tension), and a thick versus thin string (more mass); audio of each change.

exercises.idea: To make a string sound higher without fretting, do you tighten or loosen it? (tighten)
Why are the low strings thicker? (more mass per length lowers the pitch at a playable tension)
Doubling the tension raises a string by an octave (false).

lessons.title: The harmonic series
lessons.teaches: A vibrating string sounds whole-number multiples of its fundamental at once, the harmonic series, and their balance shapes its tone.
facts: A vibrating string sounds its fundamental (the main pitch you hear) plus overtones at 2, 3, 4, 5 and more times its frequency: the harmonic series.
Above the fundamental come the octave (2), the octave and a fifth (3), two octaves (4) and two octaves and a major third (5).
The balance of these harmonics is a large part of an instrument's timbre.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: string 6 drawn vibrating in one, two, three and four segments, with the nodes at frets 12, 7 and 5 marked and the matching pitches (E2, E3, B3, E4); audio.

exercises.idea: Match each harmonic number to its interval above the fundamental: 2 / octave, 3 / octave and a fifth, 4 / two octaves.
The 3rd harmonic of A2 (110 Hz) vibrates at? (330 Hz)
Bright tone (strong upper harmonics) or warm tone?

lessons.title: Natural harmonics on the neck
lessons.teaches: Touching a string lightly over a node and plucking it sounds a harmonic, and the nodes at frets 12, 7 and 5 give the octave, the octave and fifth, and two octaves.
facts: Touching a string lightly directly over a node and plucking it sounds a natural harmonic.
The harmonic at fret 12 sounds an octave above the open string, at fret 7 an octave and a fifth, at fret 5 two octaves.
On the low E string the harmonics at frets 12, 7 and 5 sound E3, B3 and E4.
The harmonic at fret 19 is the same note as at fret 7, because both lie on the nodes that divide the string into thirds.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: fretboard with harmonic diamonds at frets 5, 7, 12 and 19, each labelled with its pitch on strings 6 and 1; tab notation <12> <7> <5>; audio.

exercises.idea: Play the fret-7 harmonic on string 5 (E4) by touching the string over the fret wire.
Which fret gives a harmonic two octaves above the open string? (5)
Type the note of the fret-7 harmonic on string 4 (A).

lessons.title: Fret spacing and intonation
lessons.teaches: Each fret shortens the string by the same ratio, so frets get closer up the neck, and intonation is set by moving the saddle.
facts: Each fret shortens the vibrating string by the same ratio, about 5.6 percent, so frets get closer together up the neck.
Fret 12 sits exactly halfway between the nut and the saddle, and fret 24 three quarters of the way.
If the fretted note at fret 12 is sharp compared with the fret-12 harmonic, the saddle is moved away from the neck.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: a to-scale neck (648 mm scale) with fret distances labelled, fret 12 at 324 mm; a saddle with arrows for sharp and flat corrections.

exercises.idea: On a 648 mm scale, how far from the nut is fret 12? (324 mm)
The fretted 12th is flat against the harmonic. Move the saddle toward or away from the neck? (toward)
All frets are the same distance apart (false).

lessons.title: Equal temperament
lessons.teaches: Equal temperament splits the octave into twelve equal half steps of 100 cents, which makes every key usable at the cost of slightly impure intervals.
facts: Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve equal half steps of 100 cents each.
A pure (just) fifth, ratio 3:2, is about 2 cents wider than the equal-tempered fifth; a pure major third, ratio 5:4, is about 14 cents narrower.
Fretted instruments use equal temperament because the frets fix the same half steps in every key.
That is why tuning by matching the harmonics at frets 5 and 7 leaves each string about 2 cents off: it tunes neighbouring strings a pure fourth apart (ratio 4:3), not a tempered one.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: a cents ruler for one octave with the equal-tempered and pure fifth and major third marked; on the neck, the fifth A2-E3 (open string 5 with string 4 fret 2) and the major third E3-G#3 (string 4 fret 2 with string 3 fret 1); audio comparing a pure and a tempered major third.

exercises.idea: How many cents are in an octave? (1200)
Pure or equal-tempered major third?
An equal-tempered major third is slightly wider than a pure one (true).

lessons.title: Alternate tunings
lessons.teaches: Alternate tunings retune the open strings for new sounds, and in them the standard chord and scale shapes change.
facts: Drop D (D A D G B E) lowers string 6 a whole step; DADGAD (D A D G A D) and open G (D G D G B D) are other common tunings.
In an open tuning the open strings form a chord: open G sounds a G major chord.
Outside standard tuning, chord and scale shapes change; CAGED shapes assume standard tuning.
lessons.onTheGuitar: Figure: open-string diagrams for drop D, DADGAD and open G with retuning arrows (which strings move and by how much); audio of the open strings strummed in each.

exercises.idea: Which strings change from standard to open G? (strings 6, 5 and 1, each down a whole step)
In drop D, the open strings 6, 5 and 4 form a D5 power chord (true).
In drop D, play a D5 power chord with one finger across strings 6, 5 and 4 at fret 0, then at fret 2 (E5).
